<a id="lemma-f1c11-same-source-regional-algebra-and-affiliated-stress"></a>**Lemma F.1c.11 (Same-source regional algebra and affiliated stress).**

#### F.1c.11 — R1. Same-clock field and its actual causal commutator

Put $\omega(p)=(M^{2}+|p|^{2})^{1/2}$ and use measure $d^{3}p/(2\pi)^{3}$. Let $h_f(p)=\sqrt{\hbar/(2\omega(p))}\int f(t,x)\exp(i\omega(p)t-ip\cdot x)\,dt\,d^{3}x$. On the vacuum one-particle space, the real smeared scalar is $\Phi(f)=a(h_f)+a^*(h_f)$, with the convention that $a$ is antilinear. Its time is the actual time in $\exp(-itH/\hbar)$, $H=d\Gamma(\hbar\omega)$, obtained from the positive transfer with $\tau=\hbar t_{\mathrm{transfer}}$. It is not the update index of the sampler.

At finite lattice the identical expansion with $\omega_{a}$ and the finite Fourier sum follows by diagonalizing the actual $H_{a}$. Consequently

$$
\begin{aligned}
[\chi_a(t,x),\chi_a(s,y)] &= i \hbar E_a(t-s;x,y)\, I, \\
E_a(t;x,y) &= -[\sin(t \sqrt{A_a})/\sqrt{A_a}]_{x,y}/a^3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.1c.11.R1}
$$

In the continuum,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(t,x)&=- \int \exp(i p\cdot x) \sin(\omega(p)t)/\omega(p)\, d^3p/(2\pi)^3, \\
[\Phi(f),\Phi(g)]&=i \hbar E(f,g)\, I.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.1c.11.R2}
$$

This fixes the sign by $[\chi(0,x),\partial_t\chi(0,y)]=i\hbar\delta(x-y)$. The distribution $E$ solves $(\partial_t^{2}-\Delta+M^{2})E=0$, with $E(0)=0$ and $\partial_t E(0)=-\delta$. The KG energy identity on a truncated backwards light cone gives finite propagation: for compact initial data the energy outside its unit-speed causal development stays zero. Applying this to approximations of $\delta$ proves $\operatorname{supp}E$ is contained in the closed light cone. Therefore $E(f,g)=0$ for spacelike separated supports. This is a property of the same limiting commutator, not an imposed relativistic identification.

A continuous-time nearest-neighbor oscillator lattice generally has small nonzero commutator tails outside a light cone; exact finite-stage spacetime microcausality is NOT asserted. Equal-time disjoint-site commutation is exact. Distributional convergence $E_{a}$ to E, proved by the mode estimates in R4, supplies exact continuum microcausality.

#### F.1c.11 — R2. The actual thermal representation and regional algebra

Let $n(p)=(\exp(\beta\hbar\omega(p))-1)^{-1}$, $u=\sqrt{1+n}$, $v=\sqrt{n}$. On the doubled one-particle space define the real-linear map

$$
k_\beta(f) = (u h_f, v \overline{h_f}).
\tag{F.1c.11.R3}
$$

On its bosonic Fock space set $\Phi_\beta(f)=a(k_\beta(f))+a^*(k_\beta(f))$ and $W_\beta(f)=\exp(i\Phi_\beta(f))$. The opposite complex structure in the second component is essential: $2\operatorname{Im}\langle k_\beta(f),k_\beta(g)\rangle=2\operatorname{Im}\langle h_f,h_g\rangle$. Thus this is the SAME CCR and same causal commutator, not two independent scalars whose commutators add. Equivalently it is the doubled-Fock $b_{\beta}$ prescription of J2. Physical time is implemented by the Liouville difference on this representation; the positive comparison energy used below is a domain tool, not a claim that the physical purifier carries negative energy.

For every open spacetime region O define

$$
A_\beta(O) = \{W_\beta(f): \text{real } f \in C_c^\infty(O)\}''.
\tag{F.1c.11.R4}
$$

This is an actual von Neumann algebra on the represented Hilbert space. Inclusion of supports proves isotony. R2 and the Weyl relations prove $[A_\beta(O_1),A_\beta(O_2)]=0$ for spacelike separated regions. Additivity follows from a smooth partition of unity on compact test supports and finite Weyl products. $\Phi_\beta((\partial_t^{2}-\Delta+M^{2})f)=0$, so the assignment factors through the actual KG equation. The usual time-slice statement also follows directly: use retarded/advanced KG solutions and a time cutoff inside a Cauchy neighborhood to replace a compact test by one supported there, modulo the KG operator. It is only claimed for regions possessing that Cauchy-neighborhood relation.

The doubled Fock vacuum $\Omega_{\beta}$ gives

 $$
 \begin{gathered}
 \langle W_\beta(f)\rangle=\exp[-\lVert k_\beta(f)\rVert^{2}/2], \\
 \lVert k_\beta(f)\rVert^{2}=\int(1+2n)|h_f|^{2}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{F.1c.11.R5}
 $$

This is the fixed-$\beta$ quasifree state of the SAME $H$; finite-box reduction of the Schur thermofield state is $\exp(-\beta H_a)/\operatorname{Tr}\exp(-\beta H_a)$. The finite thermofield-to-doubled-vacuum identification is a Gaussian unitary at each finite stage. Its infinite-volume limit is used as a representation, not as a claim of a global unitary equivalence between infinite-volume vacuum and thermal representations or a trace-class infinite-volume Gibbs density.

For the nominated smooth finite-moment classical KG solution $\chi_{\mathrm{cl}}$, the displaced state has characteristic function $\exp(i\int f\chi_{\mathrm{cl}})$ times R5. The massive smooth finite-moment initial-data assumption makes its one-particle displacement square integrable; a Weyl displacement on the doubled space implements it. Its restriction to every $A_\beta(O)$ is normal. More general locally normal coherent data would require a separate local implementability argument and are not needed here. The fixed shift $\phi=\chi+m_0$ only multiplies $W$ by $\exp(im_0\int f)$, so does not change any regional algebra. Curvature signature flags and scalar/reference offsets also leave the flat field algebra unchanged.

#### F.1c.11 — R3. Local support is a label property, not norm continuity

The spacetime label $f$ has its declared material coordinates and actual clock, and R4 assigns it to every $O$ containing $\operatorname{supp}f$. Limits need not identify a test's Fourier support with its spacetime support. For fixed $f$ and a bounded physical time interval, local spatial sampling of $f$ and actual $H_{a}$ evolution define $\Phi_a(f)$. Their mode coefficients converge to R3. Preparation circuits outside observation compacts, purifier/residual storage, and inverse-coded statistical history observables remain the distinct supported source factors in P10/J5. R4 is the physical scalar regional algebra; it does not silently place an earlier history record or arbitrary preparation gate inside $O$.

Weyl labels are strongly continuous in the one-particle norm in a regular representation. They are not norm-continuous: generally $\lVert W(k)-W(l)\rVert=2$ for distinct nonzero displacement difference. Accordingly every limit below is strong on vectors or weak for the nominated states; no assertion takes operator-norm differences of distinct Weyl labels to zero.

#### F.1c.11 — R4. Actual field/state and finite-MPU comparison

Use the physical lattice dispersion and momentum-bin isometries of S5 for both thermal copies. The compact mass gap gives uniform bounds for $u_a,v_a$ and their derivatives on each retained momentum block; their high-energy thermal parts decay exponentially. A compact smooth spacetime $f$ has, uniformly in $a$, arbitrarily rapid one-particle momentum decay after time smearing. This follows from integration by parts in the physical time at $\omega_a(p)$, using $\omega_a(p)\ge c(1+|p|)$; spatial aliases are bounded by further derivatives of $f$. On $|p|\le R$, consistent dispersion/quadrature gives a polynomial error. A deliberately loose sufficient bound, for $R\ge 1$ in fixed length units, is

 $$
 \lVert k_{\beta,a}(f)-k_\beta(f)\rVert\le C_f(aR^{8}+R^{-8})+\epsilon_a.
 \tag{F.1c.11.R6}
 $$

Here $\epsilon_{a}$ contains the independently selected finite-box/bin quadrature errors. The exponents are intentionally weaker than the linear-field estimate: pointwise Taylor error is bounded by $C_{f}aR^{5}$, integration in three dimensions costs only $R^{3/2}$, and all tail powers are available. With $R=(\ell_0/a)^{1/16}$, R6 is $O(\sqrt{a/\ell_0})+\epsilon_a$. Only the continuum spatial sampling limit is involved in this estimate; finite-register errors are selected afterward as described below.

On finite-particle vectors, $\lVert(\Phi(k)-\Phi(l))\Psi\rVert\le 2\lVert k-l\rVert\,\lVert(N+1)^{1/2}\Psi\rVert$. This proves field convergence on the common core. Duhamel's identity for the exponentials, or the explicit Weyl displacement formula, then gives strong $W_a(f)$ to $W_\beta(f)$. The estimate on a fixed finite-particle $\Psi$ is $C_{\Psi,K}\lVert k-l\rVert$ when $\lVert k\rVert,\lVert l\rVert\le K$; the exponential translates $N$ by a bounded displacement. Uniform boundedness extends strong convergence to every vector. Products of finitely many Weyl operators converge strongly by telescoping; their nominated characteristic functions and all finite Weyl correlations converge. R5 also gives direct covariance/state convergence, including a converging classical displacement.

At a fixed spatial stage there are finitely many physical and purification modes. Apply the tensor-Hermite common diagonal of Lemma F.1c.2a to the actual preparation, Schur encoder, Trotter correction, physical oscillator evolution on the retained time interval, and coherent displacements. Each is a genuine finite-register unitary generated by the compressed local polynomial, not the compression of a unitary. Equations (F.1c.2a.8)–(F.1c.2a.10) control weighted vectors and first metric jets. To include $W_a(f)$, append its finite-stage real linear generator to the finite test program, or use strong-resolvent convergence of the finite linear compressions. These test exponentials do not assert finite-dimensional exact CCR.

For the encoded state include the normalized purification estimate (F.1c.2a.12) and Gibbs tail estimate (F.1c.2a.13) of Lemma F.1c.2a; a finite spectral-prefix statement alone would not control thermal trace normalization. All finite reference modes, archives and preparation resources are retained. Increase the finite register until each retained weighted field/stress/state/jet error is $\le\epsilon_a$. The physical $H_{a}$ and finitely many mode vectors then embed into the common doubled representation. This is an owned comparison of the actual source, not replacement by a second independently prepared thermal model. No uniform cost or register-size bound is claimed.

A countable dense family of tests in each compact-support smooth-test space, smooth compact-momentum finite-particle vectors, and smooth classical data gives a single exhaustion. Uniform bounds by finitely many test seminorms, as in R6 and R7 below, extend the result to all compact tests by density. These bounds are needed; convergence on a countable list alone would not establish an operator-valued distribution.

#### F.1c.11 — R5. Quadratic stress: domain and essential self-adjointness

Let D be the algebraic finite-particle domain whose wavefunctions have every polynomial momentum-weighted L2 norm. Let

$$
A=1+d\Gamma(\omega\oplus\omega).
$$

$M>0$ implies $N+1\le C_M A$. $D$ is an invariant core for $A$ and for the quadratic compact-smeared stress of S12/J2, with the actual sign of the registered improvement. Thermal subtraction, the material reference and scalar geometric offsets add real multiples of identity after smearing. Coherent shifts add a real linear field and a real scalar, with the same estimates.

For real $f$ the symmetric quadratic operator has a number-preserving part $d\Gamma(K_f)$, pair creation/annihilation parts $B_{f}$ and $B_f^*$, and optional linear/scalar terms. The following are stronger bounds than merely saying the pair kernel is Hilbert–Schmidt:

 $$
 \begin{gathered}
 \lVert T(f)\Psi\rVert\le C_f\lVert A\Psi\rVert, \\
 |\langle T(f)\Psi,A\Psi\rangle-\langle A\Psi,T(f)\Psi\rangle|\le C'_f\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{F.1c.11.R7}
 $$

Here is a direct kernel verification. The ordinary number-preserving kinetic kernel is bounded by

 $$
 C_{L}\sqrt{\omega(p)\omega(q)}(1+|p-q|)^{-L}.
 $$

Mass and improvement terms satisfy the same bound: move the improvement derivatives onto $f$, leaving the Wick square; each new test derivative is a fixed smooth compact coefficient. Dividing on the right by $\omega(q)$ leaves at most the ratio $\sqrt{\omega(p)/\omega(q)}$, bounded by $C(1+|p-q|)^{1/2}$. Schur's integral bound for $L$ sufficiently large proves $\lVert K_f\omega^{-1}\rVert<\infty$. The same Schur test gives $\lVert\omega^{-1/2}K_f\omega^{-1/2}\rVert<\infty$. These two bounds imply $\lVert d\Gamma(K_f)\Psi\rVert\le C\lVert d\Gamma(\omega)\Psi\rVert$: in the squared norm the diagonal particle terms are bounded by $C^{2}\omega_i^{2}$; cross terms are bounded in form by $C^{2}\omega_i\omega_j$ using the sandwich bound on each of the two distinct tensor factors. Summing gives $C^{2}(\sum_i\omega_i)^{2}$. This avoids an erroneous particle-number factor from a triangle inequality.

For the commutator form, divide $(\omega(p)-\omega(q))K_f(p,q)$ by $\sqrt{\omega(p)\omega(q)}$. Since $|\omega(p)-\omega(q)|\le|p-q|$, Schur gives $\lVert\omega^{-1/2}[\omega,K_f]\omega^{-1/2}\rVert<\infty$. Second quantization proves the corresponding $A$-form bound. In the doubled thermal representation same-copy terms obey this estimate. Cross-copy terms with a thermal factor have exponential decay on one leg and rapid spatial-difference decay on the other, as in J4, and satisfy the same weighted estimates.

The pair kernels and $(\omega(p)+\omega(q))B_f$ are Hilbert–Schmidt, with arbitrary further polynomial weights when needed, by the sum-frequency estimate S21 and thermal cross estimate J4. Pair-creation norms on the $n$-particle sector are bounded by $C\lVert B_f\rVert_2(n+2)$. For their commutator with $A$ use the energy-weighted pair kernel. Cauchy–Schwarz between neighboring sectors gives a quadratic-form bound $C\langle\Psi,(N+1)\Psi\rangle$, hence $C\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$. Linear terms obey the same inequalities by the one-particle weighted norm and the standard creation bound. These arguments prove R7 with constants controlled by finitely many compact-test seminorms.

The precise theorem used is Reed and Simon (1975, Theorem X.37, pp. 197–198), the operator-bounded commutator criterion. In the notation here: a symmetric operator on an operator core of a self-adjoint $A\ge 1$ is essentially self-adjoint if its norm is bounded by a constant times $\lVert A\Psi\rVert$ and its commutator quadratic form is bounded by a constant times $\lVert A^{1/2}\Psi\rVert^{2}$. R7 verifies exactly these two hypotheses; merely an $A$-form bound for $T$ would not suffice for this version.

Nelson's commutator criterion applied to $A$ and the invariant core $D$ therefore proves that each real $T(f)$ is essentially self-adjoint on $D$. Denote its closure by $\overline{T(f)}$. This step is necessary: Hilbert–Schmidt pair kernels and closability alone would not prove self-adjointness or spectral affiliation. Complex tensor tests are treated as real and imaginary parts, not as self-adjoint observables. The same argument proves invariance and domain bounds for the real Wick square with differentiated tests used by the improvement.

#### F.1c.11 — R6. Affiliation with the actual local algebra

Let $\operatorname{supp}f$ be a compact subset of $O$. Choose $\epsilon$ smaller than its distance to the boundary of $O$. Point-split the symmetrized products entering $T(f)$, using a real symmetric smooth mollifier in the relative spacetime variable, and keep both arguments inside $O$. Subtract the SAME thermal two-point function (or the explicitly registered vacuum/reference difference) before taking the diagonal. Derivatives may act on either argument. This yields a smooth compact two-variable quadratic smearing with support in $O\times O$.

Approximate that real symmetric two-variable test in its smooth topology by finite sums of symmetrized real separated tests $g_j(x)h_j(y)$, all supported in $O$. Each corresponding operator is a real finite quadratic polynomial in $\Phi_\beta(g_j),\Phi_\beta(h_j)$, plus a scalar. Its closure is self-adjoint: on the finite-dimensional one-particle complex span of these labels it is an ordinary finite-mode real quadratic, with finite Hermite analytic vectors; it acts as identity on the complementary Fock factor. To establish membership in the *local real-label algebra*, not merely the larger complex-span Fock algebra, polarize each symmetrized cross term into real squares: $\{\Phi(g),\Phi(h)\}/2=[\Phi(g+h)^{2}-\Phi(g-h)^{2}]/4$. Each $\Phi(r)$ is affiliated with $A_\beta(O)$ by its local Weyl group; hence $\exp(itc\,\Phi(r)^{2})$ belongs to $A_\beta(O)$ for every real $c$. Write the finite quadratic as a finite sum of these signed squares plus a scalar (and local linear terms if present). On its common finite-mode analytic core the derivative at zero of the product of their unitary groups is $iT_j$. The unitary Chernoff/product formula, using essential self-adjointness of this finite quadratic, gives $\exp(it\overline{T}_j)$ as a strong limit of the repeated finite products. Thus its unitary group and spectral calculus belong to $A_\beta(O)$. This also handles degenerate real spans which do not contain all canonical quadratures; membership is not inferred from the larger complex-span Fock factor alone.

Choose the finite-rank approximation and then $\epsilon$ along a diagonal so that these local self-adjoint quadratics $T_{j}$ converge to $T(f)$ on every vector of the common test core. The proof of this convergence is the same kernel domination as S21/J4: the center-coordinate time transform still sees the sum energy in vacuum pair terms; Fourier transforms of the relative mollifier are bounded uniformly and tend to one; number kernels have the spatial-difference bounds with uniform polynomial weights. For each fixed $\epsilon$, smooth finite-rank approximation converges in the required kernel/weighted norms. Derivatives of the test and the reference contractions are retained, so there is no discarded contact term.

Since $T(f)$ is essentially self-adjoint on $D$ and $T_{j}$ are self-adjoint, convergence on that core implies strong-resolvent convergence to $\overline{T(f)}$. Thus $(T_j-i)^{-1}$ converges strongly to $(\overline{T(f)}-i)^{-1}$. Every approximating resolvent belongs to $A_\beta(O)$; this von Neumann algebra is strongly closed, so the limiting resolvent belongs to it as well. Therefore

$$
\overline{T(f)} \text{ is affiliated with } A_\beta(O).
\tag{F.1c.11.R8}
$$

Real local scalar counterterms preserve affiliation. Smooth coherent shifts yield the same conclusion either by the preceding linear-term argument or by the displacement automorphism, which preserves each regional algebra up to scalar Weyl phases. Arbitrary auxiliary stress is not absorbed into R8: a nonzero auxiliary sector needs its own local assignment/limit, or the already declared zero observation Hamiltonian and retained deterministic flag/reference sector.

#### F.1c.11 — R7. Quantitative stress and locality comparisons; what is closed

For each retained compact-momentum finite-particle vector and test, the actual lattice first-vertex stress satisfies the existing S20/J5 bound

 $$
 \lVert(T_{\beta,a}(f)-T_\beta(f))\Psi\rVert\le C_{f,\Psi,\beta}\sqrt{a/\ell_0}+\epsilon_a.
 \tag{F.1c.11.R9}
 $$

R7 supplies the uniform weighted extension to $D$ and the real closure; R8 supplies affiliation. The same common diagonal includes the finite-MPU errors in $\epsilon_{a}$ and retains coherent linear/classical contributions and all first metric contacts. The separate $O(a)$ mean first-variation estimate in J14 is not replaced by the weaker R9 rate.

For spacelike separated $f,g$, R6 and the bounded one-particle norms give $|E_a(f,g)|\le C_{f,g}(\sqrt{a/\ell_0}+\epsilon_a)$. The ideal oscillator Weyl relation therefore gives

 $$
 \lVert[W_a(f),W_a(g)]\rVert\le\hbar|E_a(f,g)|\to 0.
 \tag{F.1c.11.R10}
 $$

This is a scalar commutator-phase estimate for those ideal oscillator Weyls, NOT operator-norm convergence of Weyl labels. For actual finite-MPU approximants only the corresponding represented strong/core comparison is claimed; exact finite CCR is unavailable. The limiting locality is exact by R2.

The finite support map is explicitly a common-Cauchy-slice construction. At each spatial stage, $x$ owns one oscillator factor at the selected initial physical slice; $\chi_a(t,x)=\exp(itH_a/\hbar)\chi_a(0,x)\exp(-itH_a/\hbar)$ is its actual Heisenberg evolution. A spacetime test is the time integral and spatial cell pairing of these evolved operators. Operators at distinct timelike events are not assigned independent tensor factors. The positive Euclidean history registers, archives and Schur residuals are separate actual factors and their retained statistical observables use the inverse encoder. Neither their factorization nor their Euclidean labels identify them with independent physical timelike field sites.

The retained core/service flags, purifier, and material reference data keep their own support/algebra record: preparation/routing supports precede the moving observation window; the retained purifier and residual modes have their registered storage sites and zero observation Hamiltonian when that is the declared source; persistent charged flags remain at their declared sites and supply their deterministic reference-sector stress. On the complete apparatus Hilbert space the physical net can be amplified by the identity on these retained factors. If additional local apparatus observables are included, they belong to a separately recorded auxiliary local algebra; no arbitrary nonlocal auxiliary observable is assigned to every region. A mathematical scalar material-reference functional contributes an identity-valued local stress distribution, not a new quantum field factor.

Closed here: the same massive scalar's actual regional algebra; isotony, locality, regularity, additivity and the indicated time-slice property; the same-source fixed-beta/coherent state; field/Weyl/state precursor convergence; common weighted stress OVD convergence; real self-adjoint stress closures and regional affiliation. The result supplies the narrow represented regional/stress object needed by F05 directly. It does not assert equality with the particular literal event-local finite-site assignment used in F.1/F.2, or an F.0 exact point-fibre embedding. Those stronger finite-net premises require their own check.

Not closed by Lemma F.1c.11: a universal F01 owner theorem; an operator-norm F10.1/F10.2 quotient; arbitrary nonlinear curved state/stress construction; a new auxiliary-source admission theorem; the full global action recovery/price/signature conjunction. Their separate obligations cannot be discharged merely by the existence of this free regional net.

#### F.1c.11 — R8. Fixed periodic spatial box: literal common Euclidean/physical branch

For the common compact Euclidean source in F.1c.14, take its fixed spatial torus $T^{3}_{L}$ and Euclidean temporal circumference $\beta\hbar$. The corresponding physical spacetime is the ultrastatic cylinder $\mathbb{R}\times T^{3}_{L}$, with unrestricted real physical time. Periodicity of the Euclidean preparation history is not periodicity of physical time. This fixed-box branch is sufficient for the literal common-source identification; an increasing-volume limit is optional.

Every preceding construction and proof specializes directly. Replace momentum integrals by $L^{-3}$ sums over $p=2\pi n/L$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}$, and take spatial tests smooth periodic with compact support only required in physical time (or compact support inside a chosen open spacetime region). The field map $h_{f}$ uses spatial torus integration. The one-particle space is the corresponding weighted $\ell^{2}$; finite spatial lattices embed their retained Fourier modes into these same continuum modes, so no momentum-bin interpolation or increasing-volume step is required. The mesh $a=L/m$ tends to zero at fixed $L$. The finite Hermite/source diagonal remains unchanged.

The causal kernel is the unique cylinder KG solution with initial data $(0,-\delta_{T^{3}})$, equivalently the periodization of R2. Finite propagation gives support in the cylinder causal cone, whose spatial distance is the torus geodesic distance. Thus locality holds for spacelike separation in the cylinder geometry, including its actual winding causal paths; no nonphysical Minkowski no-wrap condition is imposed for long time intervals. The region net, thermal/coherent state, point-split stress affiliation, and exact Ward identities use that same cylinder geometry.

The discrete Fourier Schur sums and weighted Hilbert–Schmidt sums obey the preceding bounds, with constants allowed to depend on $L$. Counting modes below $R$ costs $O_L(R^{3})$; hence the deliberately conservative low/high split $aR^{8}+R^{-8}$ and rate $\sqrt{a/\ell_0}$ still suffice. On this fixed-box version $\epsilon_{a}$ contains only finite source/register/time/test errors, not an infinite-volume comparison error. The thermal covariance and mean are the same discrete sums produced by the fixed-volume Schur encoder. Its reference coefficients must therefore use these fixed-$L$ means, rather than replacing them by infinite-volume integrals before a separately chosen large-box limit.

Accordingly the direct regional/stress theorem can be consumed on exactly $\mathbb{R}\times T^{3}_{L}$ with the same Euclidean torus source, $\beta$, spatial box, curvature flag, material reference and physical initial boundary. The $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ theorem above is a separate controlled large-box specialization, not a required substitution of the source used in the compact global recovery argument.

<a id="lemma-f1c12-moving-preparation-support-and-retained-apparatus"></a>**Lemma F.1c.12 (Moving preparation support and retained apparatus).**

#### F.1c.12 — A1. A completely finite stage

Fix one finite spatial/coordinate-grid field source, one finite Euclidean path-record grid, the finite sampler budget and all required controller/old-port registers. At this stage everything is finite-dimensional. The field Hamiltonian is the actual local matrix in S1–S2 of F.1c.4; the path law is the actual finite sampler or conditional-source law proved in X01's positive transfer construction. Finite mixing, acceptance, truncation and boundary errors remain the actual errors of that source, not an exact Gaussian law by declaration.

Use distinct register factors for the field and its classical path records. Euclidean history labels are recorded data coordinates; independent timelike records are not identified with the same persistent noncommuting physical oscillator. The physical regional net uses the actual oscillator registers on a common Cauchy slice and their real local evolution. The transfer/reflection theorem is the explicitly supplied correlation/generator comparison, not a pointwise tensor-factor identification.

Choose a local circuit preparing the finite actual field ground vector, and the implemented positive sampler record law, to their prescribed errors. All pure blanks, old ports and retained failures are counted. A finite global preparation unitary can be compiled into finite local gates with routed swaps on the finite connected physical graph; its finite duration, controls and support are recorded. No efficiency or cutoff-independent circuit-length claim is made. Fixed bounded gate amplitudes may be used by allowing longer durations. The final field loading stroke and its exact vacuum energy remain in the energy ledger.

The record registers have the expressly registered zero storage Hamiltonian after their gates finish. This is source data, not deletion of a nonzero physical energy. If a particular implementation has nonzero memory rest/storage energy, its actual scalar or fluctuating contribution must be added; the theorem cannot dilute it by calling the record inactive.

#### F.1c.12 — A2. Exact real preparation and its first mean contact

A normalized strictly positive finite vector $\psi(g)$, such as the unique coordinate-grid ground vector or a square-root probability vector, can be prepared by a smooth finite product $O_{g}$ of real plane rotations acting on a real blank. Use an enlarged unused coordinate if needed; this permits an orientation-preserving orthogonal path even when a chosen permutation has determinant $-1$. On a compact finite parameter domain, all partial norm denominators are positive and the rotation coefficients and their retained derivatives are bounded. These bounds may depend on the finite cutoff.

Let $O_g(t)$ be the actual real orthogonal gate path. Its finite self-adjoint generator is

$$
K_g(t)=i \hbar\, \dot O_g(t)\, O_g(t)^{\mathsf T}.
\tag{F.1c.12.A1}
$$

The evolving state is real. Since $\dot{O}O^T$ and every parameter derivative of $K/i$ are real antisymmetric,

$$
\langle\psi_g(t),K_g(t)\psi_g(t)\rangle=0,\quad\langle\psi_g(t),\partial_g K_g(t)\psi_g(t)\rangle=0.
\tag{F.1c.12.A2}
$$

These are exact identities. They also hold for controlled real rotations of a real joint sampler/record purification and for real mixed states. Thus this implementation has no hidden mean dynamical/Berry phase from those pulses. It does have nonzero pulse variance, gate strength, clock duration and initial pure-resource cost. Adding a positive scalar baseline to a signed gate generator adds its real scalar work/phase and must be recorded separately.

Conditional random choices can be realized by real rotations of fresh blank coins followed by real controlled permutations into retained output/archive registers. A projective readout can be represented by a further real pointer-copy unitary. No reset or discarded outcome is free. This supplies an actual real dilation, not a claim that an arbitrary black-box sampler has A2.

A field loading stroke $\lambda(t)H_{\mathrm{field}}$ generally has nonzero work, even when the prepared vector is its ground state. Its mean loading energy is the actual $E_0$ and its reference phase is kept. A2 does not apply to that stroke by pretending $H_{\mathrm{field}}$ is an imaginary antisymmetric preparation generator.

#### F.1c.12 — A3. A common moving preparation schedule

For stage h, let $D_{h}$ be the complete finite preparation/routing/loading duration obtained above. Choose a physical $T_{h}$ tending to infinity and place all of these executed strokes in

$$
[-T_h-D_h,-T_h].
\tag{F.1c.12.A3}
$$

Their starting resources are owned incoming finite states, and their final pointers, flags and records are retained. After $-T_h$, the actual Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{\mathrm{obs},h}=H_{\mathrm{field},h}+E_{\mathrm{ready},h} I+H_{\mathrm{other},h}.
\tag{F.1c.12.A4}
$$

Here $H_{\mathrm{other},h}$ is zero only for the explicitly zero-storage factors. Known deterministic geometry/service stocks are part of $E_{\mathrm{ready},h}$ on their actual ready sector, not part of the vanished pulse Hamiltonian. Any populated failure/unready branch has its actual separate source record and cannot be replaced by the ready scalar.

The finite field state is its actual ground state and therefore is stationary after loading. If the source preparation has an error, choose it in the prescribed energy/metric-weighted finite prefix, not only in unweighted trace distance. The latter alone cannot control a growing ultraviolet stress. The common inner-cutoff construction permits the weighted error $\epsilon_{h}$ to be prescribed before choosing the finite circuit precision.

<a id="lemma-f1c15-actual-area-port-capacity-and-purification-entropy"></a>**Lemma F.1c.15 (Actual area-port capacity and purification entropy).**

Let $s(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\rho\log\rho$ be dimensionless entropy in nats and $S=k_B s$. Let $H_2(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)$. Physical heat $Q$ is in joules; $\beta=(k_B T)^{-1}$. #### F.1c.15 — 1. Exact operational capacity and actual entanglement

<a id="theorem-f1c15a-binary-pure-output-overlap"></a>**Theorem F.1c.15a (binary pure-output overlap).**
For $0<p<1/2$ let $B=\mathbb{C}^2$ and define a memoryless cq channel with classical alphabet $\{-1,+1\}$ by

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_p(x)&=|\psi_x(p)\rangle\langle\psi_x(p)|, \\
|\psi_x(p)\rangle&=\sqrt{1-p}\,|0\rangle+x \sqrt{p}\,|1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Its unassisted reliable classical capacity, with collective output decoding allowed, is

$$
C(W_p)=H_2(p)=s(\rho_p),\qquad \rho_p=\operatorname{diag}(1-p,p).
$$

The maximizing input is uniform. The statement uses the operational asymptotic coding capacity, not one-shot accessible information. The actual purification

$$
\begin{aligned}
|\Psi_p\rangle&=\bigl(|{+1}\rangle_A|\psi_+(p)\rangle_B+|{-1}\rangle_A|\psi_-(p)\rangle_B\bigr)/\sqrt{2} \\
&=\sqrt{1-p}\,|{+}\rangle_A|0\rangle_B+\sqrt{p}\,|{-}\rangle_A|1\rangle_B
\end{aligned}
$$

has Schmidt entropy $H_2(p)$. Here $|\pm\rangle_A$ are the orthonormal Hadamard basis of the input-label register. Consequently, for every differentiable $p(s)$ in $(0,1/2)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
d\, C(W_{p(s)})/ds &= d\, s(\rho_{p(s)})/ds \\
&= \log((1-p)/p)\, p'(s),
\end{aligned}
$$

and the same derivative is the entanglement first variation of $|\Psi_{p(s)}\rangle$.

For any finite set J and parameters $p_{j}$, the product cq channel satisfies

$$
\begin{aligned}
C\Bigl(\bigotimes_{j\in J}W_{p_j}\Bigr) &= \sum_j H_2(p_j) \\
&= s\Bigl(\bigotimes_j \rho_{p_j}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

All subset restrictions commute exactly: deleting input coordinates and partially tracing the corresponding output and purification registers gives the family on the retained subset. Entropy and capacity are exactly additive on disjoint subsets.

**Proof.** For prior probability t on +1 the average output has diagonal entries 1−p,p and off-diagonal entry (2t−1)sqrt(p(1−p)). Its eigenvalue separation is

$$
\sqrt{(1-2p)^{2}+4(2t-1)^{2}p(1-p)}.
$$

The binary entropy of its eigenvalues is maximized uniquely at $t=1/2$. Each conditional signal is pure, so its Holevo information is precisely its average-output entropy. The finite-alphabet, finite-dimensional, stationary memoryless cq coding theorem gives the operational capacity equal to this optimized Holevo information. Its assumptions hold here: two specified density matrices, tensor-product word states and unrestricted collective POVMs; no entangled encoder inputs or auxiliary entanglement are used. Purification and differentiation are explicit calculations.

For a product channel every signal word is again pure. For any possibly correlated prior, subadditivity bounds average-output entropy by the sum of marginal entropies, each at most $H_2(p_j)$. The product-uniform prior attains the bound. Apply the same cq coding theorem to the finite product alphabet. Partial trace of tensor products proves the subset claim. ∎

**Primary imported theorem P1.** Holevo (1998), main unnumbered theorem, equation (5); reliable-code interpretation in equations (3)–(4), and achievability estimate (19). The paper uses bits; multiply by log 2 to obtain nats. Only this coding theorem is imported; geometric, derivative, heat and error claims below are proved here.

<a id="theorem-f1c15b-reliable-coded-output-not-only-a-source-distribution"></a>**Theorem F.1c.15b (reliable coded output, not only a source distribution).**
Let $W=\bigotimes_j W_{p_j}$. A length-$m$ code has $M$ equiprobable messages, pure product signal words and average decoding error $e$. If $\rho_{\mathrm{code}}$ is its actual average quantum output, then

$$
(1-e)\log M-H_2(e) \le s(\rho_{\mathrm{code}}) \le \log M.
$$

Thus a capacity-achieving sequence has $s(\rho_{\mathrm{code}})/m\to C(W)$. The purification obtained by coherently retaining its message label has exactly $s(\rho_{\mathrm{code}})$ entanglement entropy. For arbitrary specified physical gaps $E_{j}$, every codeword has energy exactly

$$
m \sum_j E_j p_j
$$

under the additive output Hamiltonian $\sum_{r=1}^m\sum_j E_j|1\rangle\langle 1|_{r,j}$. In particular this mean-energy equality holds at every finite block length without taking a coding limit.

**Proof.** Fano's inequality gives accessible message information at least $\log M-H_2(e)-e\log(M-1)$, hence the displayed weaker lower bound. The Holevo bound for the pure codeword ensemble is $s(\rho_{\mathrm{code}})$. Mixture entropy is at most the classical mixing entropy $\log M$, proving the upper bound. Coding at rates increasing to $C$ and errors decreasing to zero gives the limit. Every $\pm$ signal has the same diagonal populations, proving the energy equality independently of code statistics. The message-retaining vector is a purification. ∎

In the coherent preparation, A is an actual initialized and retained quantum reference controlled by the encoder; B is the receiver output. Measuring A in its label basis gives the cq ensemble. A classical mixed-message use and a coherent entangled-reference use are distinct preparations with the same B reduction. The receiver is not assumed to possess A, and neither the existence nor the accessibility of an uncharged purification resource is assumed.

<a id="theorem-f1c15c-logarithmic-dilution-and-uniform-first-variation"></a>**Theorem F.1c.15c (logarithmic dilution and uniform first variation).**
There is $\varepsilon_n\to 0$ with $\varepsilon_n=O(\log L_n/L_n)$, depending only on $c,C,g$, such that

**Proof.** Put $r=a/v_n\in[c,C]$. For $p=\gamma a/L_n$,

$$

### F.9.2 The Spin-Statistics Theorem

<a id="theorem-f2-spin-statistics-connection"></a>**Theorem F.2 (Spin-Statistics Connection).**
Assume the local net has been promoted through Definition F.0h to a relativistic AQFT $(\mathfrak A,\mathcal H,U)$ satisfying the Haag--Kastler axioms and, in addition, admits a Wightman realization with:
1. a unitary representation of the cover of the proper orthochronous Lorentz group acting covariantly on fields,
2. a unique invariant vacuum $\Omega$,
3. the spectrum condition, and
4. spacelike commutativity of the observable net and, for each retained nonzero Wightman field multiplet and its adjoint, a definite Bose-or-Fermi spacelike exchange alternative whose sign is not fixed in advance by the observable-net axiom.

Then fields transforming under integer-spin representations of the Lorentz group satisfy Bose-Einstein statistics, while fields transforming under half-integer-spin representations satisfy Fermi-Dirac statistics.

Formally, let $\phi_a$ be a nonzero tempered Wightman field on the common invariant Wightman domain, transforming in the finite-dimensional Lorentz representation $(j_1,j_2)$. The restriction of this representation to rotations contains spins
$$
j=|j_1-j_2|,|j_1-j_2|+1,\ldots,j_1+j_2,
$$
all of which have parity $(-1)^{2(j_1+j_2)}$. For spacelike-separated test-function supports, the field and its adjoint satisfy graded locality with Bose sign when $j_1+j_2\in\mathbb Z$ and Fermi sign when $j_1+j_2\in\mathbb Z+\tfrac12$:
$$
[\phi_a(f),\phi_b^\dagger(g)]_{\mp}=0.
\tag{F.9.1}
$$

*Proof.* On this conditional Wightman branch, assume a positive-metric Hilbert space, a cyclic invariant vacuum, the forward-cone spectrum, finite-component Lorentz-cover covariance, a common invariant field domain, and the Bose/Fermi spacelike exchange alternative in item 4. Let $P\in\{0,1\}$ encode the assumed Bose/Fermi sign of a field and its adjoint, and let $J$ denote its rotation-spin parity. Fewster (2016a, §3.1, Eqs. (16)–(22)) gives the Wightman/Burgoyne analytic-continuation identity $\|\phi^\dagger(f)\Omega\|^2=(-1)^{P+2J}\|\phi(Rf)\Omega\|^2$. Positivity and the nontrivial-field condition exclude the wrong sign, so $P=2J\pmod 2$. All rotation spins in the Lorentz multiplet $(j_1,j_2)$ have parity $2J=2(j_1+j_2)\pmod 2$, yielding (F.9.1) with the Bose sign for integer parity and the Fermi sign for half-integer parity. This conclusion is conditional on a Wightman field realization; spacelike commutativity of the observable net alone supplies neither that realization nor the field-level Bose/Fermi alternative. ∎

### F.9.3 PCE Interpretation of the Spin-Statistics Connection

Beyond the standard AQFT proof, the PU framework offers an independent, information-theoretic perspective on *why* nature employs distinct statistics for integer and half-integer spin fields.

<a id="proposition-f2-dimension-reduction-in-bose-and-fermi-sectors"></a>**Proposition F.2 (Dimension Reduction in Bose and Fermi Sectors).**
Let $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{single}}$ have finite dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}$. The totally antisymmetric and totally symmetric $N$-particle subspaces have dimensions
$$
\dim\bigwedge^N\mathcal H_{\mathrm{single}}
=
\binom{d_{\mathrm{int}}}{N},
\qquad
\dim\operatorname{Sym}^N\mathcal H_{\mathrm{single}}
=
\binom{d_{\mathrm{int}}+N-1}{N},
$$
respectively. Both are subspaces of the unsymmetrized tensor product of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}^N$.

*Proof.* A basis of $\bigwedge^N\mathcal H_{\mathrm{single}}$ is indexed by strictly increasing $N$-tuples of one-particle basis labels, giving $\binom{d_{\mathrm{int}}}{N}$ basis vectors. A basis of $\operatorname{Sym}^N\mathcal H_{\mathrm{single}}$ is indexed by occupation vectors $(n_1,\ldots,n_{d_{\mathrm{int}}})$ with $n_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i n_i=N$; the stars-and-bars count is $\binom{d_{\mathrm{int}}+N-1}{N}$. These counts establish compression relative to a labeled tensor-product description. They do not establish a PCE minimizer unless a common predictive task and an explicit $C_{\mathrm{agg}}$ functional are supplied. The spin–statistics assignment remains the conclusion of Theorem F.2. ∎

**Remark F.2a (Pauli Exclusion and Bures Channel Packing).** Pauli exclusion in this appendix is derived from antisymmetry together with the spin-statistics branch: for a fermionic one-particle vector $|a\rangle$,
$$
|a,a\rangle=-|a,a\rangle
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|a,a\rangle=0.
$$
A common semidefinite proof primitive can be stated without identifying the two mechanisms. For any positive state $\omega$ on a unital $*$-algebra and any finite family $\{a_i\}$, the matrix
$$
G_{ij}:=\omega(a_i^*a_j)
$$
is positive semidefinite because, for $a(z):=\sum_i z_i a_i$,
$$
z^*Gz=\omega\!\left(a(z)^*a(z)\right)\ge0.
$$
On a CAR realization with $\{c_i,c_j^*\}=\delta_{ij}\mathbf1$ and one-particle matrix $\gamma_{ij}:=\omega(c_i^*c_j)$, positivity applied to $a(z):=\sum_i z_i c_i$ gives
$$
z^*\gamma z=\omega(a(z)^*a(z))\ge0,
\qquad
z^*(I-\gamma)z=\omega(a(z)a(z)^*)\ge0,
$$
and therefore $0\preceq\gamma\preceq I$. In a Delsarte-type spherical-code certificate, a positive-definite zonal kernel likewise gives a positive-semidefinite matrix on the code points, while its normalized constant component and the off-diagonal sign constraint produce the scalar ceiling (Delsarte, Goethals and Seidel 1977).

This identifies positivity plus normalization as a shared proof pattern. The CAR unit term and the constant component of a spherical kernel have different types and supply no physical mode-to-cell map. The tangent-cell packing result of Theorem Z.10 remains a distinct finite-response statement about non-overlapping operational distinguishability cells in QFI/Bures geometry. A derivation of Pauli exclusion from channel packing requires an additional branch map identifying identical-fermion occupation cells with the tangent cells of Theorem Z.10.

<a id="theorem-f3-conditional-removal-of-response-null-permutation-multiplicity"></a>**Theorem F.3 (Conditional Removal of Response-Null Permutation Multiplicity).**
Let one retained $N$-particle sector decompose as
$$
\mathcal H_\lambda^{(N)}
\cong
\mathcal K_\lambda\otimes\mathbb C^{d_\lambda},
$$
with the permutation group acting irreducibly on the second factor. Suppose every retained observable, update, charge transporter, fusion intertwiner, and admissible protocol acts as an operator on $\mathcal K_\lambda$ tensored with $I_{d_\lambda}$. Suppose also that the protocol-response presheaf after tracing out $\mathbb C^{d_\lambda}$ is isomorphic to the original one. Then the multiplicity factor is response-null and PPI identifies the sector with its reduced description on $\mathcal K_\lambda$.

*Proof.* For every retained density matrix $\rho$ and observable $A=A_\lambda\otimes I_{d_\lambda}$,
$$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)
=
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[
\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb C^{d_\lambda}}(\rho)A_\lambda
\right].
$$
The same identity holds after every retained update and composition because those maps act trivially on the multiplicity factor. The assumed presheaf isomorphism therefore preserves every finite protocol response, including fusion and transport responses. By the PPI response-equivalence rule, the multiplicity factor is response-null and may be omitted from the reduced description. This result does not exclude parastatistics sectors whose multiplicity participates in retained fusion, gauge, localization, or transport data. ∎

### F.9.4 The CPT Theorem

<a id="theorem-f4-conditional-wightman-cpt-invariance"></a>**Theorem F.4 (Conditional Wightman CPT invariance).**
Assume the emergent AQFT admits a four-dimensional, positive-metric Wightman field realization: the fields are tempered operator-valued distributions on a common invariant domain; the vacuum is invariant and cyclic for the field algebra; the proper orthochronous Poincaré group acts covariantly; each field multiplet carries a finite-dimensional Lorentz representation; the translation spectrum lies in the closed forward cone; spacelike-separated fields obey the appropriate Bose/Fermi graded locality relations; and the field family contains the adjoint of each field. Then an antiunitary operator $\Theta_{CPT}$ on the vacuum Hilbert space fixes the vacuum and implements CPT on this field family. For a single scalar field (with its adjoint in the family), a choice of phase convention gives

$$
\Theta_{CPT}\phi(x)\Theta_{CPT}^{-1}=\eta_\phi\phi^\dagger(-x),\qquad |\eta_\phi|=1.
\tag{F.9.2}
$$

Here $\phi^\dagger$ is the Hilbert-space adjoint field. For spinor or tensor multiplets the transformation includes the representation-dependent finite-dimensional intertwiner between the multiplet and its conjugate; a universal scalar phase is not asserted.

*Proof.* Let $W_n$ denote every vacuum $n$-point distribution of fields from the adjoint-closed family. Forward-cone spectral support gives analytic continuation in the primitive forward tube of the difference variables. Finite-dimensional Lorentz covariance then permits the Bargmann–Hall–Wightman continuation to the extended tube; the spectrum condition alone does not give that larger domain. Its real points are the Jost configurations. At these points graded locality gives the required weak local commutativity, including the field-order signs. Complex Lorentz inversion and analytic continuation extend the resulting reversed-order, conjugate-field relation to the Wightman distributions, with the finite-dimensional spin/tensor intertwiners retained (Jost 1957; Hall and Wightman 1957; Wightman 2000, pp. 210–211; Borchers 1999, §4, pp. 47–48).

On the dense span of field-polynomial states $A\Omega$, define the conjugate-linear CPT map using that reversed-order relation. Equality of all Wightman inner products makes it an anti-linear isometry; cyclicity and closure of the adjoint field family make its extension antiunitary and yield the stated field transformation. The conclusion is conditional on the Wightman realization and its listed hypotheses; it does not construct that realization from the AQFT net or discharge the independent effective-action CPT gate C4-F011. ∎

### F.9.5 Relationship to PU's Fundamental Time Asymmetry

There is no contradiction between CPT symmetry and a separately selected thermodynamic orientation. Theorem 31 constrains the heat of a registered irreversible reset; it does not by itself choose a history measure, boundary condition, or time orientation. The two levels are therefore:

1. **Dynamical level (field equations):** Theorem F.4 establishes CPT symmetry on its Wightman/Jost realization branch. The effective action $S_{\mathrm{eff}}$ of Section F.5 and its field equations have this symmetry when their identification with that realization includes a CPT-covariant action representation.

2. **Thermodynamic ensemble level:** On a branch carrying independent low-boundary data, a trajectory measure, and an orientation rule, the selected ensemble may privilege entropy-increasing histories. A registered reset inequality then constrains those histories. Neither `Evolve` nor the reset bound alone breaks CPT or selects which allowed histories are realized.

**Analogy:** Time-reversal- or CPT-symmetric dynamics can permit paired histories. An independently specified low-boundary/trajectory-measure/orientation record may weight one thermodynamic direction, after which registered resets on that ensemble obey $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{reset}}\ge H_q(P\mid R)$. The inequality constrains the selected branch.

<a id="theorem-f5-consistency-of-cpt-symmetry-with-thermodynamic-irreversibility"></a>**Theorem F.5 (Consistency of CPT Symmetry with Thermodynamic Irreversibility).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem F.4, CPT is a symmetry of the emergent local dynamics. If asymptotic in/out states and an $S$-matrix exist and the CPT antiunitary preserves their domains, CPT also gives the usual conjugation relation between scattering amplitudes. These symmetry statements do not select a probability measure on histories or a thermodynamic orientation.

*Proof.* Theorem F.4 supplies an antiunitary CPT operator intertwining the local field algebra and its dynamics. Under the additional scattering hypothesis, applying this antiunitary to matrix elements between in/out states yields the CPT-conjugate amplitude relation. A symmetry maps allowed states and histories to allowed states and histories; it does not assign their statistical weights. Selection of an entropy-increasing ensemble therefore requires independent boundary or trajectory-measure data. ∎

**Remark F.CPT.1 (Orientation Interpretation).** A choice of boundary data may distinguish histories only after a separate trajectory measure and orientation rule are supplied; this is not a consequence of spectral CPT invariance alone.

<a id="theorem-f5a-conditional-modular-spin-statistics-cpt-descent-gate"></a>**Theorem F.5a (Conditional Modular Spin–Statistics–CPT Descent Gate).** On a four-dimensional regular AQFT branch, assume an irreducible local observable net of von Neumann algebras, an invariant vacuum vector $\Omega$ cyclic for the algebras of spacelike cones, and the following sector and descent data:

1. Haag duality and the split property on the retained local net (additional branch gates, not hypotheses needed for the source theorem below);
2. each retained sector $\rho$ is an irreducible, localized, transportable, Poincaré-covariant DHR morphism with finite statistics and a conjugate;
3. $\Omega$ is cyclic and separating for every retained wedge algebra; a faithful finite PCE/KMS regulator state alone does not supply this vacuum modular datum;
4. for every wedge $W$, the modular group of $(\mathfrak A(W),\Omega)$ acts on all local algebras as the correctly normalized pure Lorentz boosts preserving $W$ (modular covariance);
5. the corresponding wedge modular conjugations implement the wedge reflections on the observable net;
6. the separately defined modular cocycle obstruction of Theorem F.10.11b vanishes on the wedge/diamond cover used for branch descent.

Then for every such irreducible sector $\rho$, the modular spin–statistics relation gives
$$
\kappa_\rho=U_\rho(2\pi)=(-1)^{2s_\rho},
\qquad
\lambda_\rho=\frac{\kappa_\rho}{d_{\mathrm{stat}}(\rho)}.
\tag{F.9.5a.1}
$$
Thus the $2\pi$ rotation fixes the statistics sign, not the statistical dimension. Under the Doplicher–Roberts reconstruction hypotheses, the charged-field net has ordinary Bose/Fermi graded commutation, with the gauge representation carrying multiplicity. The modular reflection gives an antiunitary CPT action on the observable net and maps sector classes to conjugate classes. A CPT action on charged fields additionally requires the reconstructed field net and the compatible modular extension described in Guido and Longo (1995, §§2–3). These modular conclusions may replace an appeal to Wightman/Jost for the stated spin–statistics and CPT claims; they do not establish a Wightman field realization.

*Proof.* Guido and Longo (1995, Theorems 3.2 and 3.3) prove observable-net CPT and $U_\rho(2\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_\rho)$ for an irreducible local modular-covariant net and an irreducible covariant localized morphism of finite statistics. Their §3 uses Doplicher–Roberts field reconstruction to identify $d_{\mathrm{stat}}(\rho)=|\lambda_\rho|^{-1}$ and the gauge-multiplicity space; combining this with the sign equality gives (F.9.5a.1). Their §2 states the additional field-net locality and modular-covariance assumptions used for field CPT. Conditions 1 and 6 are separate branch/descent requirements and are not inferred from the Guido–Longo theorem. If the obstruction in condition 6 is nonzero, the local modular data fail the manuscript's global descent gate, independently of the source spin–statistics theorem. ∎

<a id="proposition-f5a1-fusion-and-dimension-data-do-not-fix-exchange-sign"></a>**Proposition F.5a.1 (Fusion and Dimension Data Do Not Fix Exchange Sign).** The symmetric unitary tensor categories $\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb Z_2)$ and $\mathrm{sVec}$ have the same simple-object census
$$
\{\mathbf1,x\},
\qquad
x\otimes x\cong\mathbf1,
\qquad
d_{\mathrm{stat}}(\mathbf1)=d_{\mathrm{stat}}(x)=1,
\tag{F.9.5a.1.1}
$$
and the same conjugation rule $\bar x=x$, but their self-exchange morphisms differ:
$$
c_{x,x}=+\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}
\quad\hbox{in }\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb Z_2),
\qquad
c_{x,x}=-\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}
\quad\hbox{in }\mathrm{sVec}.
\tag{F.9.5a.1.2}
$$
Therefore fusion rules, conjugates, and statistical dimensions alone cannot derive a Bose/Fermi sign. A retained exchange or modular-reflection datum is logically necessary.

*Proof.* Both categories have the two displayed simples and fusion table. In the ordinary representation category the symmetric flip acts as $+1$ on the tensor square of the nontrivial one-dimensional representation. In super-vector spaces the graded flip contributes $(-1)^{1\cdot1}=-1$ on the odd line. Hence every datum in (F.9.5a.1.1) agrees while (F.9.5a.1.2) differs. ∎

**Definition F.5b (Finitely Generated DHR-Tannaka Response Datum).** On a regular AQFT branch satisfying the Mosco-Bochner bridge of Definition F.0c and Theorem F.0d, distinguish a finite list of generating sectors from its full tensor closure, which may have infinitely many inequivalent simple sectors. Its objects have finite statistical dimension, but the category need not have finitely many simple objects;

:=

the compact group of unitary monoidal natural automorphisms of the fiber functor.

<a id="theorem-f5a2-same-dirac-reflection-cone-and-retained-fermionic-exchange"></a>**Theorem F.5a.2 (Same-Dirac Reflection, Cone and Retained Fermionic Exchange).**

#### F.5a.2.1 Original scope and source identity

#### F.5a.2.2 Carrier, locality and positive energy

Write $D=-i\alpha\cdot\nabla$, with Hermitian Clifford matrices, and $S_t=\exp(-itD)$. Let $c(f)$ be antilinear in $f$ and satisfy $\{c(f),c(g)^*\}=\langle f,g\rangle I$. The vacuum covariance is $\omega(c(f)^*c(g))=\langle g,Qf\rangle$, $Q=P_-(D)$. The physical Heisenberg flow is

On particle-hole Fock space over $H_+\oplus\overline{H_-}$, the Hamiltonian is second quantization of $|D|$ on particles and holes. The corresponding momenta are $p$ for particles and $-p$ for holes. Each excitation therefore has future null energy-momentum; finite sums and their spectral closure lie in the closed future cone. The vacuum has zero energy. Smooth compact Cauchy data have finite energy moments, although the vectors $P_\pm f$ themselves are not compactly supported.

The spacetime field is the massless Dirac Wightman field, including its adjoints. Use the algebraic Wightman domain generated by finite products of Schwartz-spacetime-smeared fields and their adjoints acting on the vacuum. It is invariant under that field family and Poincaré transformations. These bounded fermionic smearings, covariance, temperedness and the invariant cyclic vacuum meet the F.4 Wightman route. #### F.5a.2.3 Compact high-frequency Dirac pulse with a uniform transmitted contrast

Fix $R>0$ once and for all. The common base clock is $\tau=R$, $c=1$. Let $f$ be a real radial $C_c^\infty(B_1)$ function with $L^2$ norm one. For example normalize $\exp[-1/(1-|x|^2)]$ on $|x|<1$. Put $C_1=\lVert\nabla f\rVert_2$, $C_2=\lVert\Delta f\rVert_2$, $K=32(C_1+C_2+1)$. Fix $a\le R/16$, $n\in S^2$, choose a unit spinor $u_{n}$ with $(\alpha\cdot n)u_n=u_n$, and set

$$
\begin{aligned}
k&=KR/a^{2}, \\
F_a(x)&=a^{-3/2}f(x/a) \exp(ik\, n\cdot x)\, u_n, \\
G_a(x)&=F_a(x-Rn), \\
h_a&=S_{-R}G_a, \\
r_a&=\langle F_a,h_a\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

These are full local CAR modes with compact Cauchy data, not projected positive-energy modes. Define the comparison packet $T_RF_a(x)=F_a(x-Rn)$.

For Fourier variable $p=kn+q$ with $|q|\le k/2$, write $e^{-it\alpha\cdot p}=e^{-it|p|}P_+(p)+e^{it|p|}P_-(p)$. Since $P_-(kn)u_n=0$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert P_-(kn+q)u_n\rVert&\le 2|q|/k, \\
0\le|kn+q|-(k+n\cdot q)&\le|q|^{2}/k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently the pointwise difference between the exact evolution multiplier and $\exp[-it(k+n\cdot q)]u_n$ is at most $4|q|/k+t|q|^2/k$. On $|q|>k/2$ its norm is at most two; the $L^2$ tail is at most $8\lVert\Delta(a^{-3/2}f(\cdot/a))\rVert_2/k^2$. Plancherel and the triangle inequality give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lVert S_RF_a-G_a\rVert_2 \\
&\le 4C_1/(ka)+RC_2/(ka^{2})+8C_2/(k^{2}a^{2}) \\
&\le C_1/(4K)+C_2/K+C_2/(32K^{2})<1/8.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.5a.2.1}
$$

Thus $|r_a|\ge 7/8$ and $d_a:=|r_a|^2\ge 49/64$. These estimates are independent of direction. Rotation covariance, radial $f$ and $u_n^*\alpha\cdot p\,u_n=n\cdot p$ also show that the exact response quantities below are direction-independent; no global continuous choice of a spinor eigenvector on $S^2$ is needed.

The negative-energy occupancy is small but not identically zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_a&=\omega(c(F_a)^{*}c(F_a))=\lVert QF_a\rVert^{2}, \\
\lVert QF_a\rVert&\le 2C_1/(ka)+4C_2/(k^{2}a^{2}), \\
q_a&\le 1/16, \\
q_a&\to 0 \text{ as } a\to 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.5a.2.2}
$$

The same $q_{a}$ is the vacuum occupancy of $h_{a}$, since $Q$ commutes with $S_{t}$ and spatial translations. For $h_\perp=h_a-r_aF_a$ define

$$
\begin{aligned}
b_a&=\langle h_\perp,Qh_\perp\rangle,\quad 0\le b_a\le 1-d_a, \\
b_a&\le 4q_a\to 0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.5a.2.3}
$$

The bound $b_a\le 1-d_a$ uses $0\le Q\le I$ and $\lVert h_\perp\rVert^2=1-d_a$; the second bound is the squared triangle inequality after applying $Q$.

A limit exists without altering the outcomes by classical relabeling. In the normalized Fourier variable $Q'=aq$, dominated convergence gives, up to complex conjugation from the convention for $r_{a}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_a\to r_\infty &= \int |\hat{f}(Q')|^{2} \\
&\qquad \exp[-i |Q'_\perp|^{2}/(2K)]\, d^{3}Q'/(2\pi)^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{F.5a.2.4}
$$

Indeed $P_+(kn+Q'/a)u_n\to u_n$, $P_-u_n\to 0$, and
$R(|kn+Q'/a|-k-n\cdot Q'/a)\to|Q'_\perp|^2/(2K)$. The integrand is dominated by $|\hat{f}|^2$. Equation (F.5a.2.1) implies $|r_\infty|\ge 7/8$. Set $d_\infty=|r_\infty|^2>0$.

#### F.5a.2.4 Positive-duration, parity-safe preparation and measurement

Set $\varepsilon=a/4$ and $\ell=\varepsilon/3$. Use a classical input register $M$, two fermionic source reservoir modes $a_0,d_0$ initially in the fixed-parity state $|0,1\rangle$, a source dephasing qubit $E$ initially zero, receiver pointer $P$ initially zero, and record $C$ initially zero. They are actual finite apparatus degrees of freedom.

### Source, times 0 through ε

1. On $[0,\ell]$, dephase $M$ by a CNOT to $E$ and discard $E$. The Hamiltonian $\pi(I-U_{\mathrm{CNOT}})/(2\ell)$ has norm $\pi/\ell$. This gives the stated endpoint CPTP map even for arbitrary quantum/reference inputs. For classical inputs this step is redundant but retained in the resource budget.
2. On $[\ell,2\ell]$, condition on input $M=1$ and implement the fermionic mode exchange of $a_0$ and $d_0$ with Hamiltonian

   |1\rangle\langle 1|_M \otimes \pi(n_{a_0}+n_{d_0}-a_0^* d_0-d_0^* a_0)/(2\ell).

   Its norm is $\pi/\ell$. It sends the ready reservoir to $|b,1-b\rangle$ for input $b$. Both possible reservoir states have total odd parity.
3. On $[2\ell,3\ell]$, perform the even beam-splitter stroke with interaction-picture Hamiltonian

   $$
   H_A^I=\pi[c(F_a)^* a_0+a_0^* c(F_a)]/(2\ell).

   Its norm is $\pi/(2\ell)$. Its propagator exchanges the source mode and reservoir mode up to phases, and resets the field mode's occupation to $b$. Cross covariances between that mode and every orthogonal field mode are removed exactly because the reservoir initial state is independent and has zero odd expectation.

The physical lab smearing in step 3 at time $s$ is $S_sF_a$. Since $\alpha_s(c(S_sF_a))=c(F_a)$, the displayed interaction-picture Hamiltonian is exact, including free drift. Finite propagation puts its support inside $B_{a+\varepsilon}(0)$. This is a positive-duration local source control, not an instantaneous odd-field kick.

### Receiver and commit, times R−2ε through R

In $[R-2\varepsilon,R-\varepsilon]$ use the time-dependent lab mode $S_{t-R}G_a$. Its interaction-picture version is exactly $c(h_a)$, and its spatial support is inside $B_{a+2\varepsilon}(Rn)$. Set $n_h=c(h_a)^*c(h_a)$. The even measurement coupling is

$$

$$

Its propagator is $U_B=(I-n_h)\otimes I_P+n_h\otimes X_P$ and its norm is $\pi/\varepsilon$. It copies the actual field-mode number into $P$. In $[R-\varepsilon,R]$, copy $P$'s $Z$ value into $C$ with a CNOT Hamiltonian of norm $\pi/\varepsilon$ and discard $P$. The retained $C$ record is classical and complete at $R$. No zero-duration measurement or record copy is used. Only tick-completed records are admitted; $C$'s precommit ready value carries no input information, and intermediate readouts are not part of this protocol family.

### Exact response

The source-reset calculation and detector number readout give

$$
\Pr(C=1|M=b)=b_a+b\, d_a,\quad b=0,1.
\tag{F.5a.2.5}

This holds without assuming the original local source mode is empty or ignoring its vacuum correlations. To see it directly, $c(h_a)=\overline{r_a}c(F_a)+c(h_\perp)$. After the swap, the source term has occupation $b$, its cross terms have zero expectation, and the orthogonal-mode covariance remains $Q$. The difference of the two probabilities is exactly $d_{a}$.

For an arbitrary input density matrix $\rho_{\mathrm{MY}}$, replace old Y content by the fresh record C and trace the apparatus and field. The actual physical realization equals

\Phi_a(\rho_{MY})&=\sum_{b,y} p_a(y|b) \\
&\qquad \langle b|\operatorname{Tr}_Y(\rho_{MY})|b\rangle\, |b,y\rangle\langle b,y|, \\
L_{b,y,z}&=\sqrt{p_a(y|b)}\, |b,y\rangle\langle b,z|.

\tag{F.5a.2.6}

The Kraus list sums to identity. The equality extends with arbitrary independent reference systems, because the input was actually dephased and all instrument branches have the same conditional kernel. Other retained independent logical endpoint registers are untouched. The source field itself and discarded reservoir are not asserted to be untouched.
