<a id="theorem-f104c6-complete-reflection-test-for-simple-massive-rational-covariances"></a>**Theorem F.10.4c.6 (Complete Reflection Test for Simple Massive Rational Covariances).** Fix $d\ge1$, distinct masses $0<m_1<\cdots<m_k$, and real coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_k$. Use units $c=\hbar=1$ and the common Euclidean time coordinate $t$. On $\mathbb R^{1+d}$ let the translation-invariant tempered covariance have Fourier multiplier
$$
\widehat C(p_0,\mathbf p)=\sum_{j=1}^k\frac{c_j}{p_0^2+|\mathbf p|^2+m_j^2}.
\tag{F.10.4c.6.1}
$$
No contact term is included. Let $\mathcal D_+=C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d))$: each test has a compact positive-time support, and all spatial Schwartz seminorms of every time derivative are uniformly bounded there. With the unitary spatial Fourier transform, define the reflection form
$$
Q_C(f)=\int_{t,s>0}\!\!dt\,ds\int d\mathbf x\,d\mathbf y\,
\overline{f(t,\mathbf x)}\,C(t+s,\mathbf x-\mathbf y)f(s,\mathbf y).
$$
Then $Q_C(f)\ge0$ for every $f\in\mathcal D_+$ if and only if every $c_j\ge0$. The same equivalence holds if the tests are required to have compact spatial support. Every negative coefficient has a smooth negative-norm witness; the result covers all tests and all masses in the displayed class.

For nonnegative coefficients, omit the zero coefficients and put $\omega_j(\mathbf p)=\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+m_j^2}$. The completed one-particle reflection quotient is exactly
$$
\mathcal H_1=\bigoplus_{j:c_j>0}L^2\!\left(\mathbb R^d,\frac{c_j\,d\mathbf p}{2\omega_j(\mathbf p)}\right),
\qquad
(Vf)_j(\mathbf p)=\int_0^\infty e^{-t\omega_j(\mathbf p)}\widehat f(t,\mathbf p)\,dt.
\tag{F.10.4c.6.2}
$$
Positive-time translation by $a\ge0$ induces the strongly continuous contraction $e^{-aH_1}$, where $(H_1h)_j=\omega_jh_j$ on the multiplication-operator domain. This Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional when at least one coefficient is positive. These are one-particle covariance and transfer conclusions; a full source-to-field, instrument and continuum-net realization retains the additional entries of Definition F.0h.

In particular, every covariance
$$
\widehat C(p)=\prod_{j=1}^k(p_0^2+|\mathbf p|^2+m_j^2)^{-1},\qquad k\ge2,
\tag{F.10.4c.6.3}
$$
with distinct positive masses fails reflection positivity, although its Fourier multiplier is strictly positive at every real momentum. More generally, a nonzero covariance in (F.10.4c.6.1) that is $o(|p|^{-2})$ at large Euclidean momentum fails reflection positivity.

*Proof.* For $\omega>0$, elementary contour integration gives
$$
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{ip_0u}}{p_0^2+\omega^2}\,dp_0
=\frac{e^{-\omega|u|}}{2\omega}.
$$
For $u>0$ the upper-half-plane semicircle contributes zero because the rational denominator is quadratic and $|e^{ip_0u}|\le1$ there; the pole at $i\omega$ has residue $e^{-\omega u}/(2i\omega)$. The formula at $u<0$ follows by reflection and at zero by the elementary integral of $(p_0^2+\omega^2)^{-1}$. Partial spatial Fourier transformation therefore gives
$$
Q_C(f)=\sum_{j=1}^k\int_{\mathbb R^d}\frac{c_j}{2\omega_j(\mathbf p)}
\left|\int_0^\infty e^{-t\omega_j(\mathbf p)}\widehat f(t,\mathbf p)\,dt\right|^2d\mathbf p.
\tag{F.10.4c.6.4}
$$
All exchanges of integrals are justified here: the positive-time support is separated from zero, the spatial test is Schwartz, the masses have a strictly positive minimum, and there are finitely many summands. Each absolute integral is finite. This identity proves sufficiency and the Gram representation in (F.10.4c.6.2).

For necessity, suppose $c_{j_0}<0$. Choose a nonzero nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty))$ and define
$$
g(t)=\prod_{l\ne j_0}(\partial_t-m_l)\psi(t).
$$
Boundary terms vanish to every order. Integrating by parts gives, for each $u>0$,
$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-ut}g(t)\,dt
=\prod_{l\ne j_0}(u-m_l)\int_0^\infty e^{-ut}\psi(t)\,dt.
$$
At $\mathbf p=0$, this Laplace transform vanishes at every $m_l$, $l\ne j_0$, and is nonzero at $m_{j_0}$, since the masses are distinct and the last integral is strictly positive. Thus the continuous function
$$
B(\mathbf p)=\sum_j\frac{c_j}{2\omega_j(\mathbf p)}
\left|\int_0^\infty e^{-t\omega_j(\mathbf p)}g(t)\,dt\right|^2
$$
is strictly negative at zero. Choose a nonzero smooth compactly supported $\widehat\chi$ in a ball where $B<0$, and set $f(t,\mathbf x)=g(t)\chi(\mathbf x)$. Formula (F.10.4c.6.4) gives $Q_C(f)=\int|\widehat\chi|^2B<0$. This is an admitted smooth positive-time test. To obtain compact spatial support, let $\eta$ be smooth, compactly supported and equal to one near zero, and replace $\chi$ by $\eta(\mathbf x/n)\chi$. These products converge to $\chi$ in every Schwartz seminorm: outside a growing ball each derivative is controlled by arbitrarily high polynomial decay of $\chi$, and inside that ball the derivatives of the cutoff are either zero or have bounded powers of $n^{-1}$. The form (F.10.4c.6.4) is continuous in those seminorms. Its values therefore converge to the strictly negative value just found and are negative for all sufficiently large $n$. Necessity follows for either test class.

It remains to verify that the quotient completion is all of the displayed direct sum, rather than a proper subspace. Let $r$ be the number of positive coefficients and choose $\psi$ as above and a number $\tau>0$. Define the $r$ translates $g_l(t)=\psi(t-l\tau)$ for $l=0,\ldots,r-1$, extended by zero outside their positive-time supports. Their Laplace transforms form the matrix
$$
M_{jl}(\mathbf p)=L_\psi(\omega_j(\mathbf p))\,e^{-l\tau\omega_j(\mathbf p)}.
$$
Its first factors are strictly positive. The numbers $e^{-\tau\omega_j(\mathbf p)}$ are pairwise distinct at every finite $\mathbf p$, so the Vandermonde determinant is nonzero. The inverse matrix is smooth and bounded with all derivatives on every compact momentum set. For any vector $h=(h_j)$ of smooth compactly supported momentum functions, solve $M(\mathbf p)a(\mathbf p)=h(\mathbf p)$. The components $a_l$ are smooth and compactly supported. Taking
$$
\widehat f(t,\mathbf p)=\sum_{l=0}^{r-1}g_l(t)a_l(\mathbf p)
$$
gives $Vf=h$. Such vectors are dense in the finite direct sum of the weighted $L^2$ spaces because each weight is positive and smooth, locally bounded above and below. The Gram identity identifies the null space with $\ker V$ and proves the asserted quotient completion. Compact spatial tests have the same dense image by the Schwartz cutoff argument. If $r=0$, both the quotient and the direct sum are zero.

For $f_a(t,\mathbf x)=f(t-a,\mathbf x)$, with zero extension at $t\le a$, substitution gives $Vf_a=e^{-a\omega}Vf$. This descends through the null space and is contractive. Dominated convergence applied to $|e^{-a\omega}-1|^2|h|^2\le4|h|^2$ proves strong continuity at $a=0$. The spectral multiplication operator $H_1$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative on $\{h:\sum_j\int\omega_j^2|h_j|^2c_j/(2\omega_j)<\infty\}$; its exponentials give the stated semigroup. A positive summand contains infinitely many orthogonal functions on disjoint compact momentum sets, proving infinite dimension.

The partial fractions of (F.10.4c.6.3) have coefficients
$$
c_j=\prod_{l\ne j}(m_l^2-m_j^2)^{-1}.
$$
Multiplying by $|p|^2+m_j^2$ and evaluating at $|p|^2=-m_j^2$ proves the formula. There are $j-1$ negative factors, so $c_2<0$ when $k\ge2$, and the classification applies. Finally, the coefficient of $|p|^{-2}$ in (F.10.4c.6.1) is $\sum_jc_j$. Faster decay forces this sum to zero; nonnegative coefficients with zero sum all vanish. This proves the final assertion. ∎

The simple-pole reflection classification is the corresponding case of Arici, Becker, Ripken, Saueressig and van Suijlekom (2018), Theorem 3.7; the proof above also identifies its common one-particle quotient and transfer map. For the two-mass choice $m_1=1$, $m_2=2$, (F.10.4c.6.3) has coefficients $1/3,-1/3$. At zero spatial momentum, the two positive times $t_1=\ln2$, $t_2=2\ln2$ and coefficients $(1,-2)$ annihilate the first Laplace component and give reflection value $-1/768$. These point-time values are a finite algebraic witness; the smooth localization argument in the proof supplies the actual continuum test. A nonnegative Euclidean Fourier multiplier is therefore insufficient for the reflection gate in this exact scalar class. The finite-register Gaussian construction below supplies the Euclidean source, higher-field/domain data and common response-preserving approximation on its declared positive-mass branch.

<a id="definition-f104c7-massive-gaussian-finite-register-source"></a>**Definition F.10.4c.7 (Massive Gaussian Finite-Register Source).**

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a positive computable mass $m$. For a finite digital realization the input record includes an algorithm producing rational enclosures of $m$ and a rational lower bound $0<m_*\le m$. Set $c=\hbar=1$. Spatial Fourier transforms are unitary:

$$
\widehat g(p)={(2\pi)}^{-d/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x}g(x)\,dx.
$$

For every integer $n\ge1$ fix

$$
a_n=\tau_n=4^{-n},\quad \ell_n=16^n+1,\quad L_n=a_n\ell_n=4^n+4^{-n},\quad
\delta_n=\frac{2\pi}{L_n},\quad R_n=4^n.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.1}
$$

The spatial torus has odd side length $\ell_n$ in sites. With $b_n=(\ell_n-1)/2$, its positions and momenta are

$$
X_n=a_n{\{-b_n,\ldots,b_n\}}^d,\qquad
\mathcal P_n=\delta_n{\{-b_n,\ldots,b_n\}}^d.
$$

There are $M_n=\ell_n^d$ modes. Put

$$
\omega_n(p)={\left(m^2+4a_n^{-2}\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(a_np_j/2)\right)}^{1/2},\qquad
\mathfrak h_n=\ell^2(\mathcal P_n).
\tag{F.10.4c.7.2}
$$

The source register and its occupation basis are

$$
\mathcal H_n=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{R_n}\operatorname{Sym}^r\mathfrak h_n,
\quad
\{|\nu\rangle:\nu\in\mathbb N_0^{M_n},\ |\nu|\le R_n\},
\quad
D_n=\binom{M_n+R_n}{R_n}.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.3}
$$

Thus $\lceil\log_2 D_n\rceil$ qubits encode the register by lexicographic ranking of the finite occupation list. On padding basis states extend $H_n$ by zero and every desired unitary by the identity. The scalar baseline and padding control in Definition F.10.4c.21 and Proposition F.10.4c.22 then leave their endpoint action inactive while preserving positivity on the full qubit carrier. The vacuum is the zero-occupation vector $\Omega_n$. The Hamiltonian is the finite diagonal matrix

$$
H_n|\nu\rangle=\left(\sum_p\nu_p\omega_n(p)\right)|\nu\rangle,
\quad 0\le H_n\le E_n^{\max}I,
\quad E_n^{\max}=R_n\sqrt{m^2+4d/a_n^2}.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.4}
$$

All entries are computable from the source record. The ideal real-time and transfer matrices are $U_n(t)=e^{itH_n}$ and $T_n(s)=e^{-sH_n}$, for $t\in\mathbb R$ and $s\ge0$. Physical response queries use the clock grid $\tau_n\mathbb Z$ and round a queried time $t$ to a nearest grid value ${[t]}_n$, with $|{[t]}_n-t|\le\tau_n/2$. The continuously indexed matrices are useful in proofs and are the functional calculus of this same finite Hamiltonian.

The untruncated oscillator space $\Gamma_s(\mathfrak h_n)$ is an auxiliary proof space. It is never counted as a finite register. On it, let $a(h)$ be antilinear in $h$, let $a^*(h)$ be linear and impose $[a(h),a^*(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle$. Let $P_R$ project onto particle number at most $R$. Every source matrix below is explicitly its finite occupation-basis matrix. In particular,

$$
\phi_n(h)=P_{R_n}\bigl(a^*(h)+a(h)\bigr)P_{R_n}\big|_{\mathcal H_n}.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.5}
$$

Before truncation, inverse discrete Fourier transformation gives canonical positions $q_x$ and momenta $\pi_x$ and the normally ordered nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian

$$
\frac12\sum_{x\in X_n}\left(\pi_x^2+m^2q_x^2+
 a_n^{-2}\sum_j{(q_{x+a_ne_j}-q_x)}^2\right)-\frac12\sum_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\omega_n(p).
\tag{F.10.4c.7.6}
$$

Its diagonal form is $d\Gamma(\omega_n)$. The cutoff commutes with it. The finite source (F.10.4c.7.4) is its exact restriction, including the stated vacuum-energy subtraction.

**Local smearing and the retained readout.**

For $g\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define its periodization $g^{\mathrm{per},n}(x)=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^d}g(x+L_nz)$ and

$$
h_n(g)(p)=\frac{a_n^d}{L_n^{d/2}\sqrt{2\omega_n(p)}}
\sum_{x\in X_n}g^{\mathrm{per},n}(x)e^{-ip\cdot x}.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.7}
$$

For real $g$, $\phi_n(h_n(g))$ is the compression of $a_n^{d/2}\sum_xg^{\mathrm{per},n}(x)q_x$. If $g$ is compactly supported, the lattice weights eventually have that same spatial support, up to sampling. The global occupation cutoff still acts on the whole register.

For a real $F\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{1+d})$, use the same lattice and clock:

$$
h_n(F)=\tau_n\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}e^{ir\tau_n\omega_n}h_n(F(r\tau_n,\cdot)).
\tag{F.10.4c.7.8}
$$

Only finitely many time samples are nonzero. The bounded retained readout is

$$
K_n(F)=P_{R_n}W_n(h_n(F))P_{R_n}\big|_{\mathcal H_n},
\qquad W_n(h)=e^{i(a^*(h)+a(h))}.
\tag{F.10.4c.7.9}
$$

This is a contraction. It is specified by finite entries, without executing an infinite oscillator: for occupation multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ in (F.10.4c.7.3),

$$
\langle\alpha|K_n(h)|\beta\rangle
=e^{-{\|h\|}^2/2}
\prod_{j=1}^{M_n}
\left[
\sqrt{\alpha_j!\beta_j!}
\sum_{s=0}^{\min(\alpha_j,\beta_j)}
\frac{{(ih_j)}^{\alpha_j-s}{(i\overline h_j)}^{\beta_j-s}}
{s!(\alpha_j-s)!(\beta_j-s)!}
\right].
\tag{F.10.4c.7.10}
$$

The convention $0^0=1$ is used. Formula (F.10.4c.7.10) follows by expanding $e^{-{\|h\|}^2/2}e^{ia^*(h)}e^{ia(h)}$ between the two finite occupation vectors: the intermediate occupation $s$ cannot exceed either endpoint in each mode. The displayed sums are finite. This also identifies the source readout exactly with the compression in (F.10.4c.7.9).

The compressed Weyl readout $K_n(h)$ and the finite unitary $e^{i\phi_n(h)}$ are distinct matrices. The response grammar in this construction uses (F.10.4c.7.9). A heralded operation using it has success Kraus operator $K_n(h)$ and failure Kraus operator ${(I-{K_n(h)}^*K_n(h))}^{1/2}$; both outcomes are retained. Proposition F.10.4c.20 gives an unconditioned implementation and its complete-record error.

<a id="proposition-f104c8-same-register-reflection-quotient"></a>**Proposition F.10.4c.8 (Same-Register Reflection Quotient).** Let

$$
\mathfrak A_{E,n}=M_{D_n}(\mathbb C)\otimes {M_{D_n}(\mathbb C)}^{\mathrm{op}},
\quad \mathfrak A_{+,n}=M_{D_n}(\mathbb C)\otimes1,
$$

and define

$$
\Theta_n(A\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}})=B^*\otimes{(A^*)}^{\mathrm{op}},\qquad
\Omega_{E,n}(A\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}})=\langle\Omega_n,BA\Omega_n\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.8.1}
$$

Then $\Theta_n$ is an antilinear involutive algebra automorphism, $\Omega_{E,n}(1)=1$, and

$$
\Omega_{E,n}(\Theta_n(A\otimes1)(B\otimes1))
=\langle A\Omega_n,B\Omega_n\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.8.2}
$$

The reflection quotient is exactly $\mathcal H_n$, with quotient unitary $V_n^{\mathrm{OS}}[A]=A\Omega_n$. The positive-time transfer

$$
\mathcal T_{E,n}(A)=e^{-\tau_nH_n}Ae^{\tau_nH_n}
\tag{F.10.4c.8.3}
$$

preserves the null space, fixes $1$, and induces $e^{-\tau_nH_n}$. Left multiplication induces the exact representation of $M_{D_n}$ on $\mathcal H_n$. Its vacuum is cyclic and invariant, and its reconstructed Hamiltonian is the same $H_n$.

*Proof.* In the opposite algebra,
$(A\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}})(C\otimes D^{\mathrm{op}})=AC\otimes{(DB)}^{\mathrm{op}}$.
Applying (F.10.4c.8.1) gives $B^*D^*\otimes{(C^*A^*)}^{\mathrm{op}}$, which is the product of the two reflected factors. Antilinearity and $\Theta_n^2=I$ follow from adjunction. Formula (F.10.4c.8.2) follows by multiplying the factors and applying the functional. Thus the null space is $\{A:A\Omega_n=0\}$. Every vector is $A\Omega_n$ for a rank-one matrix $A$, so the quotient is onto. Since $H_n\Omega_n=0$, (F.10.4c.8.3) sends $A\Omega_n$ to $e^{-\tau_nH_n}A\Omega_n$. Its eigenvalues lie in $[e^{-\tau_nE_n^{\max}},1]\subset(0,1]$ and logarithmic reconstruction gives (F.10.4c.7.4). If $A\Omega_n=0$, then $BA\Omega_n=0$, so left multiplication is well defined and has the asserted representation. Finally $1$ maps to $\Omega_n$ and its translates remain fixed. ∎

For a positive-time word with $0<t_1\le\cdots\le t_r$, its matrix in this same algebra is

$$
A_w=e^{-t_1H_n}X_1e^{-(t_2-t_1)H_n}\cdots X_re^{t_rH_n}.
\tag{F.10.4c.8.4}
$$

Here each $X_j$ is a declared source field, readout or other finite matrix. Reflection gives the adjoint word in reversed order, and (F.10.4c.8.2) is exactly the corresponding reflected transfer correlation. A common translation of every $t_j$ is (F.10.4c.8.3). The apparently growing final factor in (F.10.4c.8.4) acts as the identity on the vacuum. Its correlation can therefore be evaluated using decaying transfer contractions and the finite $X_j$, as in Definition F.10.4c.21 and Proposition F.10.4c.22.

The finite Euclidean source is the matrix-history functional (F.10.4c.8.1), the class admitted by Definition F.10.4c.1. Ordinary positivity as a measure on commuting Euclidean random fields is a property of the limiting Gaussian source in Theorem F.10.4c.17. Finite reflection positivity here is the exact Gram identity (F.10.4c.8.2).

<a id="proposition-f104c9-finite-field-cyclicity-and-gaussian-moment-threshold"></a>**Proposition F.10.4c.9 (Finite Field Cyclicity and Gaussian Moment Threshold).** The vacuum is cyclic already for the unital algebra generated by the finite equal-time fields with real spatial weights. If a vacuum word has $2r$ field insertions, with arbitrary nonnegative transfer intervals between them, its value is exactly the untruncated lattice Gaussian value whenever $R_n\ge r$. Odd moments vanish. On particle sectors at most $R_n-1$, the compressed annihilation and creation commutator is the usual CCR. On the top sector,

$$
[a_R(h),a_R^*(k)]
=\langle h,k\rangle I-
P_{=R}\,a(h)a^*(k)\,P_{=R},\qquad
 a_R(h)=P_Ra(h)P_R.
\tag{F.10.4c.9.1}
$$

Consequently the finite compressed field family can have nonzero equal-time commutators for distinct lattice sites.

*Proof.* Real spatial basis weights have one-particle images whose complex span is all $\mathfrak h_n$, because the discrete Fourier transform and the positive multiplier $1/\sqrt{2\omega_n}$ are invertible. A product of $r\le R_n$ fields on the vacuum has top component $a^*(h_1)\cdots a^*(h_r)\Omega_n$ and components of smaller particle number. Induction subtracts these smaller components and generates every symmetric tensor of degree $r$. Their union is the whole finite register.

Expand a vacuum word into creation/annihilation paths. A nonzero path starts and ends at zero occupation and changes total number by one at each of its $2r$ steps. Its height never exceeds $r$; otherwise it could not return to zero in the remaining steps. Every transfer factor preserves occupation and has the same value before and after restriction. The cutoff deletes no contributing path when $R_n\ge r$. An odd path cannot return to zero. The untruncated vacuum is Gaussian by the CCR normal-ordering identity, so its even moments are the Wick pairings of its two-point function.

For (F.10.4c.9.1), expand the commutator with $I=P_R+(I-P_R)$. The term $P_Ra^*(k)(I-P_R)a(h)P_R$ is zero because annihilation lowers number. The other omitted term is supported on the top sector and equals $P_{=R}a(h)a^*(k)P_{=R}$. This proves the formula, including its support and its bound $(R+1)\|h\|\|k\|$. ∎

<a id="definition-f104c10-common-represented-gaussian-comparison"></a>**Definition F.10.4c.10 (Common Represented Gaussian Comparison).**

Let $\mathfrak h=L^2(\mathbb R^d,dp)$ and $\omega(p)=\sqrt{m^2+{|p|}^2}$. For each $p\in\mathcal P_n$, let

$$
C_{n,p}=p+{[-\delta_n/2,\delta_n/2)}^d.
$$

These cells partition $B_n={[-\pi/a_n,\pi/a_n)}^d$. The isometry $J_n:\mathfrak h_n\to\mathfrak h$ is

$$
J_ne_p=\delta_n^{-d/2}\mathbf1_{C_{n,p}},\qquad \Pi_n=J_nJ_n^*.
\tag{F.10.4c.10.1}
$$

On $\mathcal H=\Gamma_s(\mathfrak h)$ define the isometry

$$
I_n=\bigoplus_{r=0}^{R_n}J_n^{\otimes_s r},\qquad
Q_n=I_nI_n^*=\mathbf1_{\{N\le R_n\}}\Gamma(\Pi_n).
\tag{F.10.4c.10.2}
$$

All finite operators are compared through the corner representation $A\mapsto I_nAI_n^*$. Its identity is $Q_n$, and $Q_n\to I$ strongly. The centered cells need not nest. No exact finite-to-finite algebra embeddings or projective compatibility are asserted. These maps furnish one common Hilbert-space comparison on the frozen path (F.10.4c.7.1).

The continuum field and Weyl conventions are

$$
\phi(h)=a^*(h)+a(h),\qquad W(h)=e^{i\phi(h)},\qquad
W(h)W(k)=e^{-i\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle}W(h+k).
\tag{F.10.4c.10.3}
$$

For real spacetime tests, set

$$
\kappa F(p)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\omega(p)}}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\omega(p)}\widehat{F(t,\cdot)}(p)\,dt.
\tag{F.10.4c.10.4}
$$

For complex tests the field is extended complex linearly, equivalently
$\phi(F)=a^*(\kappa F)+a(\kappa\overline F)$.

<a id="lemma-f104c11-lattice-cell-and-clock-comparison"></a>**Lemma F.10.4c.11 (Lattice, Cell and Clock Comparison).** For every $g\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, uniformly on $|t|\le T$,

$$
\left\|J_ne^{i{[t]}_n\omega_n}h_n(g)-e^{it\omega}\frac{\widehat g}{\sqrt{2\omega}}\right\|
\le C_{d,m,T}\,S_{d+4}(\widehat g)\,(\delta_n+a_n^2+\tau_n),
\tag{F.10.4c.11.1}
$$

where $S_s(u)=\sup_p{(1+|p|)}^s(|u(p)|+|\nabla u(p)|)$. The same bound holds for decaying exponentials and $0\le t\le T$. For every compact spacetime test $F$ there is a finite Schwartz-seminorm constant $c_F$ such that

$$
\varepsilon_n(F):=\|J_nh_n(F)-\kappa F\|
\le c_F(\delta_n+a_n^2+\tau_n)\le c'_F4^{-n}.
\tag{F.10.4c.11.2}
$$

The constants are bounded by the displayed seminorms, support sizes and one-dimensional radial integrals; numerical computation uses the effective protocol inputs in Definition F.10.4c.21 and Proposition F.10.4c.22. No regulator-dependent constant is suppressed.

*Proof.* Write $a=a_n$, $\delta=\delta_n$, $\rho=\sqrt d\,\delta/2$ and $s=d+4$. Poisson summation gives exactly

$$
\delta^{-d/2}h_n(g)(p)
=\frac1{\sqrt{2\omega_n(p)}}\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^d}\widehat g(p+2\pi z/a).
\tag{F.10.4c.11.3}
$$

The periodization and Fourier series converge with all required derivatives because $g$ is Schwartz. On a cell with center $p$, the continuum frequency satisfies

$$
|\omega_n(p)-\omega(q)|\le\rho+\frac{a^2}{24}{|p|}^3,
\quad q\in C_{n,p}.
\tag{F.10.4c.11.4}
$$

Indeed $|2\sin(au/2)/a-u|\le a^2{|u|}^3/24$, the Euclidean norm of the vector of cubic component errors is at most $a^2{|p|}^3/24$, and $z\mapsto\sqrt{m^2+{|z|}^2}$ is 1-Lipschitz. Also $\omega_n\ge m$ and $\omega_n(p)\le m+|p|$.

The derivative of $b(v)={(2v)}^{-1/2}$ is bounded in absolute value by ${(2\sqrt2m^{3/2})}^{-1}$ for $v\ge m$. The derivative of $p\mapsto b(\omega(p))$ has the same bound, and $b\le{(2m)}^{-1/2}$. Sampling the function $b(\omega)\widehat g$ at the centers therefore incurs an $L^2(B_n)$ error bounded by

$$
\rho{(1+\rho_*)}^s\left({(2m)}^{-1/2}+{(2\sqrt2m^{3/2})}^{-1}\right)
S_s(\widehat g){\left[\int_{\mathbb R^d}{(1+|q|)}^{-2s}\,dq\right]}^{1/2},
\tag{F.10.4c.11.5}
$$

where $\rho_*=\pi\sqrt d/4$ bounds $\rho$ on the whole sequence. To see this, integrate the derivative along the segment in a cell and use $1+|q|\le(1+\rho_*)(1+|p'|)$ for every point $p'$ on that segment.

Replacing $b(\omega(p))$ by $b(\omega_n(p))$ contributes at most

$$
\frac{a^2S_s(\widehat g)}{48\sqrt2m^{3/2}}
{(1+\rho_*)}^{s+3}
{\left[\int_{\mathbb R^d}{(1+|q|)}^{6-2s}\,dq\right]}^{1/2}.
\tag{F.10.4c.11.6}
$$

Here the centerwise sum $\delta^d\sum_p{|p|}^6{(1+|p|)}^{-2s}$ is bounded by the displayed integral with the cell-comparison factor. Both integrals converge because $s=d+4$.

For $z\ne0$ and $p\in B_n$, $|p+2\pi z/a|\ge\pi{|z|}_\infty/a$. Hence the alias sum is bounded pointwise by

$$
S_s(\widehat g){(a/\pi)}^s\sum_{z\ne0}{|z|}_\infty^{-s}.
$$

The lattice sum converges since $s>d$. Multiplying by ${(2m)}^{-1/2}{|B_n|}^{1/2}$ bounds its $L^2$ contribution by a fixed constant times $a^{s-d/2}S_s$. The omitted exterior tail is bounded by

$$
{(2m)}^{-1/2}S_s{\left(\frac{|\mathbb S^{d-1}|}{2s-d}\right)}^{1/2}
{(\pi/a)}^{d/2-s}.
\tag{F.10.4c.11.7}
$$

Since $a\le1/4$ and $s-d/2>2$, both terms are bounded by a constant times $a^2S_s$.

For the time factor, $|e^{itu}-e^{itv}|\le T|u-v|$ and $|e^{i{[t]}_nu}-e^{itu}|\le\tau_nu/2$. Apply (F.10.4c.11.4) to the continuum vector, whose weighted ${|q|}^3$ and $|q|$ norms are bounded by the same seminorm and convergent radial integrals. The inequalities for $e^{-tu}$ are identical for nonnegative $u,v,t$. This proves (F.10.4c.11.1).

Finally, integrate the spatial estimate over the compact time support of $F$. The time Riemann-sum error is at most $\tau_n$ times the time-support length enlarged by $2\tau_n$, times the supremum of the $L^2$ norm of the time derivative of $e^{it\omega}\widehat F_t/\sqrt{2\omega}$. This derivative is $e^{it\omega}(i\omega\widehat F_t+\partial_t\widehat F_t)/\sqrt{2\omega}$, with a finite uniform Schwartz bound. The same estimate applies to the spatially sampled integrand, or follows by adding and subtracting its continuum value at each time sample. This proves (F.10.4c.11.2). ∎

<a id="definition-f104c12-gaussian-response-state-domain"></a>**Definition F.10.4c.12 (Gaussian Response-State Domain).**

Define the positive one-particle form

$$
\mathsf A=1+{|p|}^2-\Delta_p,
\qquad
\mathsf K=d\Gamma(\mathsf A),
\quad
\mathcal Q=\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf K^{1/2}).
\tag{F.10.4c.12.1}
$$

This dense form domain contains all finite-particle Schwartz vectors and the vacuum. A response-state record is a density matrix $\rho$ satisfying $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\mathsf K)\le E<\infty$. It supplies particle number, momentum second moment and momentum-gradient control on one and the same state. In particular it supplies finite mean physical energy because $\omega(p)\le m+|p|\le(m+1)(1+{|p|}^2)$.

<a id="lemma-f104c13-regular-state-projection-budget"></a>**Lemma F.10.4c.13 (Regular-State Projection Budget).** For every $\psi\in\mathcal Q$,

$$
\|(I-Q_n)\psi\|\le q_n\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|,
\qquad
q_n={\left(\frac{d\delta_n^2}{\pi^2}+\frac{a_n^2}{\pi^2}+\frac1{R_n+1}\right)}^{1/2}
\le C_d2^{-n}.
\tag{F.10.4c.13.1}
$$

*Proof.* Cellwise Neumann Poincaré, or the cosine expansion on a cube of side $\delta_n$, bounds the squared error of cell averaging by $\delta_n^2\pi^{-2}\int{|\nabla f|}^2$ on that cell. The slightly looser factor $d$ in (F.10.4c.13.1) remains valid. On $B_n^c$, $|p|\ge\pi/a_n$, so the exterior squared error is at most $a_n^2\pi^{-2}\int {|p|}^2{|f|}^2$. These bounds add because interior and exterior are orthogonal. For an $r$-particle tensor, $I-\Pi_n^{\otimes r}\le\sum_{j=1}^r{(I-\Pi_n)}_j$ as commuting positive projections. Apply the one-particle form inequality to each coordinate and sum over $r$. The number tail is $\mathbf1_{\{N>R_n\}}\le N/(R_n+1)$. The two projections commute, and $I-Q_n\le I-\Gamma(\Pi_n)+\mathbf1_{\{N>R_n\}}$. Taking expectations gives the square of (F.10.4c.13.1). ∎

Particle or physical-energy bounds without momentum regularity do not give a uniform cell-projection rate: in a fixed low-energy momentum ball, normalized smooth functions can be orthogonal to every cell constant. For arbitrary finite-energy states the exact projection tail remains in the estimates below. Strong convergence still follows from $Q_n\to I$, first on compactly supported smooth finite-particle vectors and then on every vector by density and $\|Q_n\|\le1$.

<a id="lemma-f104c14-ideal-operation-form-bounds"></a>**Lemma F.10.4c.14 (Ideal-Operation Form Bounds).** If $h\in\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf A^{1/2})$ and $\psi\in\mathcal Q$, then

$$
\|\mathsf K^{1/2}W(h)\psi\|
\le\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|+\|\mathsf A^{1/2}h\|\,\|\psi\|.
\tag{F.10.4c.14.1}
$$

The continuum unitary $U(t)=\Gamma(e^{it\omega})$ and contraction $T(s)=\Gamma(e^{-s\omega})$ preserve $\mathcal Q$, and for $|t|,s\le T$,

$$
\|\mathsf K^{1/2}U(t)\psi\|,
\ \|\mathsf K^{1/2}T(s)\psi\|
\le(1+T)\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|.
\tag{F.10.4c.14.2}
$$

*Proof.* For a positive one-particle form $A$, the quadratic-form norm of ${d\Gamma(A)}^{1/2}\psi$ is the Hilbert norm of the vector-valued annihilation distribution $A^{1/2}a\psi$. Weyl displacement replaces $a\psi$ by $a\psi+ih\psi$ after a unitary conjugation. The triangle inequality gives (F.10.4c.14.1), first on finite-particle smooth vectors and then by form closure. One can equivalently prove it with finite-rank bounded $A$, using ${W(h)}^*a(f)W(h)=a(f)+i\langle f,h\rangle$, and increase the form approximants to $A$.

For $U(t)$, number and momentum moments are unchanged. In each particle coordinate, differentiation gives $\nabla(e^{it\sum\omega}\psi_r)=e^{it\sum\omega}(\nabla\psi_r+it\nabla\omega\,\psi_r)$ and $|\nabla\omega|\le1$. Combine all coordinate components in one Hilbert norm and use the triangle inequality. The added norm is at most $|t|\|N^{1/2}\psi\|\le|t|\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|$. For $T(s)$ the same calculation applies, with the multiplying exponential bounded by one. ∎

<a id="lemma-f104c15-common-source-dynamics-convergence"></a>**Lemma F.10.4c.15 (Common-Source Dynamics Convergence).** Write $\widetilde U_n(t)=I_nU_n({[t]}_n)I_n^*$ and $\widetilde T_n(s)=I_nT_n({[s]}_n)I_n^*$, using nonnegative nearest grid values for $s\ge0$. For every $T<\infty$ there is an explicit constant $b_{d,m,T}$ such that

$$
\sup_{|t|\le T}\|(\widetilde U_n(t)-U(t))\psi\|
+\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|(\widetilde T_n(s)-T(s))\psi\|
\le b_{d,m,T}2^{-n}\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|.
\tag{F.10.4c.15.1}
$$

Both families therefore converge strongly, uniformly on compact time intervals, on all of $\mathcal H$.

*Proof.* On $B_n$, let $\omega_n^c(q)=\omega_n(p)$ at the cell center. Extend it by $\omega(q)$ outside $B_n$. Because $a_n|p|\le\pi\sqrt d$ in the Brillouin zone, (F.10.4c.11.4) implies, with a constant depending only on $d$,

$$
|\omega_n^c(q)-\omega(q)|\le c_d\bigl(\delta_n+a_n{|q|}^2\bigr)
\quad(q\in\mathbb R^d).
\tag{F.10.4c.15.2}
$$

For example, substitute $|p|\le|q|+\rho$ into $a_n^2{|p|}^3/24$, use $a_n|p|\le\pi\sqrt d$, and absorb $a_n\rho^2$ in $\delta_n$. The multiplication unitaries $V_n(t)=\Gamma(e^{i{[t]}_n\omega_n^c})$ commute with $Q_n$, and $\widetilde U_n(t)=V_n(t)Q_n$. For real $x,y$, ${|e^{ix}-e^{iy}|}^2\le2|x-y|$. On every particle sector, sum (F.10.4c.15.2) and the clock error. Since $\omega_n^c\le m+|q|+\rho$ in $B_n$ and equals $\omega$ outside, integration yields

$$
{\|(V_n(t)-U(t))\psi\|}^2
\le c_{d,m}(T+1)(\delta_n+a_n+\tau_n)\langle\psi,\mathsf K\psi\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.15.3}
$$

Together with (F.10.4c.13.1) and $\|V_n(t)\|=1$, this gives the unitary assertion. For nonnegative $x,y$, ${|e^{-x}-e^{-y}|}^2\le |x-y|$, and the identical argument applies to transfer contractions. All constants are independent of $n$. Since $\delta_n\le2\pi4^{-n}$, (F.10.4c.15.1) follows. Density and the uniform contraction bounds extend convergence to every vector. ∎

<a id="theorem-f104c16-summable-strong-gaussian-responses"></a>**Theorem F.10.4c.16 (Summable Strong Gaussian Responses).** Let $F$ be a real compact spacetime test, $h=\kappa F$, $h_n^c=J_nh_n(F)$ and $\widetilde K_n(F)=I_nK_n(F)I_n^*$. For every $\psi\in\mathcal Q$,

$$
\begin{split}
\|(\widetilde K_n(F)-W(h))\psi\|
\le{}&q_n\bigl(2\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|+\|\mathsf A^{1/2}h\|\|\psi\|\bigr)\\
&+\varepsilon_n(F)\bigl(2\|{(N+1)}^{1/2}\psi\|+\|h\|\|\psi\|\bigr).
\end{split}
\tag{F.10.4c.16.1}
$$

Thus $\widetilde K_n(F)\to W(\kappa F)$ strongly and the adjoints converge strongly. Every finite word of these readouts, their adjoints, the real-time matrices and the Euclidean transfers converges strongly, with a summable $C\,2^{-n}$ error on states of bounded $\mathsf K$ form norm. The constant is uniform over a fixed word length, bounded times and bounded indicated test seminorms.

*Proof.* Since $h_n^c$ belongs to $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_n$, the oscillator factorization gives exactly

$$
\widetilde K_n(F)=Q_nW(h_n^c)Q_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.16.2}
$$

Put $v=h_n^c-h$. The Weyl relation and the spectral integral identity $e^{i\phi(v)}-I=i\int_0^1e^{is\phi(v)}\phi(v)\,ds$ on its domain give

$$
\|(W(h_n^c)-W(h))\psi\|
\le\|v\|\bigl(2\|{(N+1)}^{1/2}\psi\|+\|h\|\|\psi\|\bigr).
\tag{F.10.4c.16.3}
$$

Here $\|\phi(v)\psi\|\le2\|v\|\|{(N+1)}^{1/2}\psi\|$, and the Weyl phase is bounded by $|\operatorname{Im}\langle h,v\rangle|\le\|h\|\|v\|$. Inserting $Q_n$ before and after gives an initial tail $\|(I-Q_n)\psi\|$ and a final ideal tail $\|(I-Q_n)W(h)\psi\|$, in addition to (F.10.4c.16.3). Apply (F.10.4c.13.1) and (F.10.4c.14.1). This is (F.10.4c.16.1). The adjoint is the same source expression with $-F$.

For a word $A_k\cdots A_1$, expand

$$
\widetilde A_{k,n}\cdots\widetilde A_{1,n}-A_k\cdots A_1
=\sum_{j=1}^k\widetilde A_{k,n}\cdots\widetilde A_{j+1,n}
(\widetilde A_{j,n}-A_j)A_{j-1}\cdots A_1.
\tag{F.10.4c.16.4}
$$

All finite suffix operators are contractions. Every local error is evaluated on an unprojected ideal prefix, whose form norm is bounded recursively by (F.10.4c.14.1)–(F.10.4c.14.2). Centered-cell projections need not preserve the momentum-gradient form domain, and no such preservation is used. Apply (F.10.4c.15.1), (F.10.4c.16.1), and $\|{(N+1)}^{1/2}\xi\|\le\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\xi\|+\|\xi\|$. This gives the asserted $C2^{-n}$ bound and its convergent sum. The dense-domain estimate plus uniform boundedness proves strong convergence on every vector. ∎

To compare normal states, use the specified channel

$$
\mathcal E_n(\rho)=I_n^*\rho I_n+
\operatorname{Tr}((I-Q_n)\rho)\,|\Omega_n\rangle\langle\Omega_n|.
\tag{F.10.4c.16.5}
$$

It is completely positive and trace preserving; the lost weight is retained as a vacuum-fill contribution. For $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\mathsf K)\le E$, (F.10.4c.13.1) gives lost weight at most $q_n^2E$. Integrating (F.10.4c.16.4) over a spectral decomposition of $\rho$ and using Cauchy–Schwarz gives

$$
\left|\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal E_n(\rho)A_{k,n}\cdots A_{1,n})
-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A_k\cdots A_1)\right|
\le C_{k,\mathcal F,T}(1+\sqrt E)2^{-n}+q_n^2E.
\tag{F.10.4c.16.6}
$$

The vacuum is mapped exactly. Equation (F.10.4c.16.5) is a comparison channel for supplied state data. Finite preparation of arbitrary continuum states is not required by the vacuum construction; preparation of additional source states is a separate input and its cost is charged in Definition F.10.4c.21 and Proposition F.10.4c.22.

<a id="theorem-f104c17-full-same-source-gaussian-reflection-reconstruction"></a>**Theorem F.10.4c.17 (Full Same-Source Gaussian Reflection Reconstruction).** The finite source vacuum moments converge, on the same path, to the centered Gaussian functional with covariance

$$
\widehat C(p_0,p)=\frac1{p_0^2+{|p|}^2+m^2}.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.1}
$$

This functional is a probability measure on tempered distributions. Its positive-time reflection quotient is unitarily $\Gamma_s(L^2(\mathbb R^d,dp))$, including every particle sector. Its vacuum is the Fock vacuum and its transfer semigroup is $e^{-s\,d\Gamma(\omega)}$. These identifications agree with the finite quotient maps, smearing maps, correlation limits and represented dynamics of Propositions F.10.4c.8–F.10.4c.9 and the comparison results in Definition F.10.4c.10 through Theorem F.10.4c.16.

*Proof: existence of the Euclidean source.* Put $D=d+1$. Choose a real Hermite orthonormal basis ${(e_\alpha)}_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^D}$ of $L^2(\mathbb R^D)$ and independent real standard Gaussian variables $\xi_\alpha$. With probability one, $|\xi_\alpha|\le C(1+|\alpha|)$ for some finite random $C$: the exceptional Gaussian tail probabilities are summable, because the number of multi-indices of a given total degree is polynomial. Hermite coefficients of a Schwartz function decay faster than every power of $1+|\alpha|$, by repeated application of $-\Delta+{|x|}^2$. Thus

$$
\mathcal W(f)=\sum_\alpha\xi_\alpha\langle e_\alpha,f\rangle
$$

is almost surely a continuous linear functional on Schwartz space and has covariance ${\langle f,g\rangle}_{L^2}$. The Fourier multiplier $C^{1/2}={(p_0^2+{|p|}^2+m^2)}^{-1/2}$ maps Schwartz space continuously to itself: all derivatives of its smooth symbol have polynomial bounds, and the Fourier transform preserves Schwartz space. Define $\Phi(f)=\mathcal W(C^{1/2}f)$. It is a random tempered distribution with covariance $\langle f,Cg\rangle$. Its characteristic functional is

$$
\mathbb E e^{i\Phi(f)}=\exp[-\tfrac12\langle f,Cf\rangle]
\quad(f\text{ real}).
\tag{F.10.4c.17.2}
$$

Gaussian finite-dimensional distributions determine the measure on the cylinder $\sigma$ algebra of tempered distributions. This constructs the Gaussian Euclidean source and proves its positivity.

*Proof: the reflection quotient.* For $f$ supported at positive Euclidean times put

$$
(Kf)(p)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\omega(p)}}\int_0^\infty e^{-t\omega(p)}\widehat f(t,p)\,dt.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.3}
$$

The Fourier integral in $p_0$ gives $e^{-\omega|t-s|}/(2\omega)$, so

$$
C(\theta\overline f,g)=\langle Kf,Kg\rangle.
$$

For Wick-ordered Gaussian monomials, all pairings within either reflected half have been subtracted. Hence

$$
\mathbb E\left[\Theta{:\!\Phi(f_1)\cdots\Phi(f_r)\!:}_C
\;{:\!\Phi(g_1)\cdots\Phi(g_s)\!:}_C\right]
=\mathbf1_{\{r=s\}}\sum_{\pi\in S_r}\prod_{j=1}^r\langle Kf_j,Kg_{\pi(j)}\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.4}
$$

This follows directly by differentiating the Gaussian exponential (F.10.4c.17.2) with separate source parameters in the two halves; the two Wick counterfactors cancel the within-half quadratic forms. Therefore the map

$$
{:\!\Phi(f_1)\cdots\Phi(f_r)\!:}_C
\longmapsto \sqrt{r!}\,\operatorname{Sym}(Kf_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Kf_r)
\tag{F.10.4c.17.5}
$$

is exactly an isometry after quotienting by reflection-null vectors. Wick polynomials span the polynomial algebra because normal ordering is triangular by degree.

The complex span of $Kf$ is dense in $L^2(dp)$. To prove it, choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth positive-time function $\chi$ with compact support. Its Laplace transform $L_\chi(\omega)$ is strictly positive. For any $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ choose the spatial Fourier function $\widehat g(p)=\sqrt{2\omega(p)}h(p)/L_\chi(\omega(p))$, which is smooth and compactly supported. Then $K(\chi g)=h$. Spatial cutoffs of the Schwartz function $g$ approximate it in Schwartz topology and hence under $K$, giving the same dense range with compact spatial tests. Symmetric products of a dense one-particle subspace are dense in every finite sector, and the algebraic sum of sectors is dense in Fock space. Thus (F.10.4c.17.5) is onto after completion. In particular it proves reflection positivity for all positive-time polynomial histories and identifies the full null space.

A positive-time translation by $s$ sends $Kf$ to $e^{-s\omega}Kf$ and preserves the Gaussian normal-ordering covariance by translation invariance. Equation (F.10.4c.17.5) therefore intertwines transfer with $\Gamma(e^{-s\omega})=e^{-s\,d\Gamma(\omega)}$. Its vacuum is the image of $1$, and its generator has the usual self-adjoint multiplication domain on the direct sum of particle sectors. Strong continuity follows by dominated convergence sectorwise and then by the contraction bound on the sector tail.

*Proof: identification with the finite source.* The finite untruncated two-point function, for spatial tests at Euclidean time separation $u\ge0$, is

$$
C_n(u;g,h)=\langle h_n(g),e^{-u\omega_n}h_n(h)\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.6}
$$

The first application of a field creates one particle and the second annihilates it; hence (F.10.4c.17.6) is already exact on the finite register when $R_n\ge1$. Lemma F.10.4c.11 gives uniform convergence on bounded time intervals to
$\langle\widehat g/\sqrt{2\omega},e^{-u\omega}\widehat h/\sqrt{2\omega}\rangle$, with error bounded by a fixed test seminorm times $\delta_n+a_n^2+\tau_n$. For $2r$ insertions and $R_n\ge r$, Proposition F.10.4c.9 identifies the finite moment with the sum of its $(2r-1)!!$ lattice pairings. If all pair covariances are bounded by $B$ and their errors by $\epsilon_n$, the telescoping product bound is

$$
|S_{2r,n}-S_{2r}|
\le(2r-1)!!\,r\,{(B+\epsilon_n)}^{r-1}\epsilon_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.7}
$$

For Euclidean moments, use the spatial map (F.10.4c.7.7), the ordered transfer words (F.10.4c.8.4) and the clock-grid Riemann weights; the Euclidean factor $e^{-\omega|t-s|}$ is Lipschitz in the time difference, including coincident times. A fixed ordering of coincident insertions is retained at every finite stage. Once $R_n\ge r$ its value equals the symmetric Gaussian pairing and is independent of that ordering. Compact supports and Schwartz bounds justify every sum and integral by an integrable majorant. Thus all fixed-degree source history correlations, and their reflected Gram matrices, converge to (F.10.4c.17.2)–(F.10.4c.17.4), with summable error.

There is also convergence of the history vectors under the actual embeddings, beyond convergence of their Gram matrices. For a compact positive-time test define the discrete Laplace vector

$$
K_n^+f=\tau_n\sum_{r>0}e^{-r\tau_n\omega_n}h_n(f(r\tau_n,\cdot)).
\tag{F.10.4c.17.8}
$$

Lemma F.10.4c.11 and its time Riemann estimate give $J_nK_n^+f\to Kf$ with the same summable rate. Wick-order a degree-$r$ positive-time polynomial with the discrete covariance (F.10.4c.17.6), representing its ordered words by (F.10.4c.8.4). If $R_n\ge r$, every vector path from the vacuum stays below the cutoff. Expanding and subtracting the internal pairings leaves exactly
$\sqrt{r!}\operatorname{Sym}(K_n^+f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes K_n^+f_r)$.
Under $I_n$ this converges to (F.10.4c.17.5). More precisely, writing $u_{j,n}=J_nK_n^+f_j$ and $u_j=Kf_j$, its vector error is at most

$$
\sqrt{r!}\sum_{j=1}^r\|u_{j,n}-u_j\|
\prod_{l<j}\|u_{l,n}\|\prod_{l>j}\|u_l\|.
\tag{F.10.4c.17.9}
$$

This is the tensor-product telescoping identity followed by the norm-one symmetrizer. Thus the same embeddings intertwine the finite reflection quotients and every fixed continuum Fock sector on a dense history set. Under (F.10.4c.17.5), the one-particle vectors and transfer matrices are exactly the limits of (F.10.4c.7.7), (F.10.4c.8.2) and (F.10.4c.8.3). Their symmetric products fix all sectors. The direct Fock comparison of Theorem F.10.4c.16 and the full Gaussian reflection quotient consequently have the same vacuum, correlations, transfer generator and dense history vectors. ∎

<a id="theorem-f104c18-massive-scalar-wightman-realization"></a>**Theorem F.10.4c.18 (Massive Scalar Wightman Realization).** On the Fock space in Theorem F.10.4c.17, the fields

$$
\phi(F)=a^*(\kappa F)+a(\kappa\overline F)
\tag{F.10.4c.18.1}
$$

form a scalar Wightman field on the common invariant domain

$$
\mathcal D=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}^{\mathrm{alg}}
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{sym}}({(\mathbb R^d)}^r).
\tag{F.10.4c.18.2}
$$

The vacuum is unique, invariant and cyclic. The translation spectrum lies in the closed forward cone. There is a strongly continuous unitary representation of the proper orthochronous Poincaré group, with scalar field covariance. Every vacuum distribution is tempered and is the analytic continuation of the Euclidean distribution in Theorem F.10.4c.17. The Källén–Lehmann measure, with the conventions of Corollary F.10.4c.4, is $\delta_{m^2}$ with unit positive residue and zero vacuum expectation.

The finite field matrices converge on this same domain directly. For real $F$,

$$
I_n\phi_n(h_n(F))I_n^*=Q_n\phi(J_nh_n(F))Q_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.18.3}
$$

If $\psi\in\mathcal D$ has at most $r$ particles, then for $R_n\ge r+1$ the occupation boundary is absent from this action. With $h=\kappa F$ and $h_n^c=J_nh_n(F)$,

$$
\begin{split}
\|(Q_n\phi(h_n^c)Q_n-\phi(h))\psi\|
\le{}&2\sqrt{r+1}\|h_n^c\|\|(I-Q_n)\psi\|\\
&+2\sqrt{r+1}\|h_n^c-h\|\|\psi\|+
\|(I-Q_n)\phi(h)\psi\|.
\end{split}
\tag{F.10.4c.18.4}
$$

All three terms tend to zero by (F.10.4c.11.2), (F.10.4c.13.1) and invariance of $\mathcal D$ under the continuum field. Their sum has a summable rate for each such $\psi$. Thus the field/domain identification follows from the finite matrices themselves, without differentiating a strong limit of bounded Weyl operators.

*Proof: field domain and temperedness.* The shell map $F\mapsto\kappa F$ is continuous from spacetime Schwartz space to spatial Schwartz space. Indeed derivatives of $\omega$ and $\omega^{-1/2}$ have polynomial bounds, and the spacetime Fourier transform decays faster than every power when restricted to $(\omega(p),p)$. Creation and annihilation with a Schwartz wavefunction preserve (F.10.4c.18.2), as do the Poincaré maps below. On a fixed $r$-particle vector,

$$
\|\phi(F)\psi_r\|
\le\sqrt{r+1}\|\kappa F\|\|\psi_r\|+
\sqrt r\|\kappa\overline F\|\|\psi_r\|.
\tag{F.10.4c.18.5}
$$

This proves vector-valued continuity in the Schwartz topology and the common domain. For real $F$, iterating the number bound gives

$$
\|{\phi(F)}^k\psi_r\|\le2^k{\|\kappa F\|}^k\sqrt{(r+k)!/r!}\|\psi_r\|.
$$

The power series with coefficients $z^k/k!$ converges for all $z$. The dense invariant analytic domain therefore makes the symmetric field essentially self-adjoint; its exponential is precisely (F.10.4c.10.3). The same estimate directly identifies its power series with the displacement unitary on this domain.

The two-point momentum distribution is the positive forward-shell measure

$$
W_2(x-y)={(2\pi)}^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}
\frac{e^{-i[\omega(p)(x^0-y^0)-p\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)]}}{2\omega(p)}\,dp.
\tag{F.10.4c.18.6}
$$

The measure has polynomial growth, so $W_2$ is tempered. Each even vacuum distribution is the finite sum of Wick pairings of $W_2$ and each odd one vanishes. A pairing uses every variable once; it is a tensor product of two-point distributions followed by a permutation of variables, which preserves temperedness. This supplies the full distributional growth control rather than deriving it from reflection positivity alone.

*Proof: Poincaré representation.* Write $p^+=(\omega(p),p)$ and $p'=\operatorname{spatial}(\Lambda^{-1}p^+)$. On $L^2(dp)$ set

$$
(U_1(a,\Lambda)h)(p)
=e^{ip^+\cdot a}\sqrt{\frac{\omega(p')}{\omega(p)}}\,h(p'),
\qquad U(a,\Lambda)=\Gamma(U_1(a,\Lambda)).
\tag{F.10.4c.18.7}
$$

The measure $dp/(2\omega(p))$ is Lorentz invariant: it is the result of integrating the invariant distribution $\mathbf1_{\{p^0>0\}}\delta({(p^0)}^2-{|p|}^2-m^2)\,d^{d+1}p$ in $p^0$. Thus the square-root Jacobian in (F.10.4c.18.7) makes the map unitary. Change of variables proves the group law. On compactly supported smooth wavefunctions, continuity of the transformation and its Jacobian proves strong continuity by dominated convergence; density and unitarity extend it to every vector, and finite-sector approximation proves it on Fock space. Positive mass makes the change of variables smooth with polynomially controlled derivatives and inverse, so it preserves (F.10.4c.18.2).

For $F_{a,\Lambda}(x)=F(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$, changing variables in (F.10.4c.10.4) gives

$$
\kappa F_{a,\Lambda}=U_1(a,\Lambda)\kappa F.
$$

Second quantization and the adjoint relation give scalar field covariance. Translations have joint generators $H=d\Gamma(\omega)$ and $\mathbf P=d\Gamma(p)$. On each sector their joint spectrum consists of sums of positive mass-shell vectors, hence lies in the closed forward cone. On every nonvacuum sector $H\ge m$, so $\ker H=\mathbb C\Omega$; the invariant vacuum is unique.

*Proof: cyclicity and correlation identification.* The one-particle complex span of $\kappa F$ is dense. For a compact momentum region choose a compact smooth time test whose Fourier transform is nonzero on the bounded energy range and divide by that factor to realize any smooth compact momentum vector using a Schwartz spatial test. Spatial cutoff then gives compact spacetime tests by continuity. The top component of a product of fields on the vacuum is the corresponding symmetric creation tensor; induction subtracts the lower components. Their span is dense in each sector and hence in Fock space. This proves cyclicity.

For ordered imaginary-time differences with positive real parts, (F.10.4c.18.6) becomes $e^{-u\omega}/(2\omega)$. Wick pairings then give exactly (F.10.4c.17.1) and (F.10.4c.17.6). The shell integral $W_2(z)$ is holomorphic for $z=x-iy$ with $y$ in the open forward cone: $e^{-ip^+\cdot z}=e^{-ip^+\cdot x}e^{-p^+\cdot y}$ has an exponentially decaying mass-shell multiplier. Their polynomially bounded distributional boundary values are (F.10.4c.18.6). Products on independent paired variables preserve these analytic and boundary-value properties. Thus the Euclidean and Wightman fields are two realizations of the same source correlations. Finally (F.10.4c.18.6) is the single positive mass shell with unit weight, so its spectral mass measure is $\delta_{m^2}$. Time-ordering (F.10.4c.18.6) gives the distribution with Fourier transform $i/(p^2-m^2+i0)$. Dividing this transform by $i$ gives the response convention of Corollary F.10.4c.4, namely $G^F(p^2)={(p^2-m^2+i0)}^{-1}$, with $N=0$, $P_{-1}=0$ and unit positive residue. This fixes the contact/subtraction prescription explicitly. ∎

<a id="theorem-f104c19-local-gaussian-net-and-time-slice"></a>**Theorem F.10.4c.19 (Local Gaussian Net and Time Slice).** For an open spacetime region $O$ define

$$
\mathfrak A(O)={\{W(\kappa F):F\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)\}}^{\prime\prime}.
\tag{F.10.4c.19.1}
$$

This vacuum net satisfies isotony, Einstein locality, Poincaré covariance and additivity. It has the cyclic invariant vacuum and forward-cone representation of Theorem F.10.4c.18. For a neighborhood of a Cauchy surface in a globally hyperbolic causally convex region, its algebra generates the region algebra. For every fixed finite word of local Weyl generators the finite source representatives converge strongly with the error in Theorem F.10.4c.16. If $F$ and $G$ have spacelike separated supports,

$$
[\widetilde K_n(F),\widetilde K_n(G)]\psi\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\|[\widetilde K_n(F),\widetilde K_n(G)]\psi\|
\le c_{F,G}(1+\|\mathsf K^{1/2}\psi\|)2^{-n}
\tag{F.10.4c.19.2}
$$

for normalized $\psi\in\mathcal Q$.

*Proof: locality.* The field commutator is the scalar distribution
$[\phi(F),\phi(G)]=2i\operatorname{Im}\langle\kappa F,\kappa G\rangle I$ for real tests. Its kernel is the Klein–Gordon causal propagator, obtained by subtracting the two boundary orders in (F.10.4c.18.6). It solves the Klein–Gordon equation, has zero initial position data and $\delta$ initial velocity data, up to the fixed sign convention.

Its support lies in the double light cone. One direct proof first uses smooth compact Cauchy data. The Klein–Gordon energy density is

$$
e=\tfrac12({|\partial_tu|}^2+{|\nabla u|}^2+m^2{|u|}^2),
$$

with flux $-\partial_tu\,\nabla u$ of magnitude at most $e$. Integrating the local conservation law over the exterior of the expanding support ball shows that the exterior energy cannot increase from zero; boundary flux is bounded by the outward boundary motion term. The solution vanishes outside the cone. Mollify the $\delta$ velocity data and pass to the distributional limit using the explicit Fourier solution $\sin(t\omega)/\omega$. The support statement survives this limit. Thus the commutator vanishes for spacelike separated test supports. The Weyl relation then proves commutation of the generators, and commutants are strongly closed, proving locality for (F.10.4c.19.1).

Isotony is immediate from test support. Poincaré covariance follows from (F.10.4c.18.7). For an open cover of $O$, every compactly supported test has a finite subordinate smooth partition of unity. The Weyl relation expresses its Weyl operator as a scalar times a finite product of the partitioned Weyl operators. This proves additivity after taking double commutants.

*Proof: time slice.* Let $P=\Box+m^2$ and let $E=G_{\mathrm{ret}}-G_{\mathrm{adv}}$. For $F\in C_c^\infty(O)$ set $u=EF$. Choose a smooth temporal switch $\chi$ that is zero to the past of the chosen Cauchy neighborhood and one to its future, with derivative supported inside that neighborhood on the causal support of $F$. Global hyperbolicity and compact support make the relevant causal slab compact; a smooth choice exists by a finite partition of unity on this slab. Put

$$
F'=P(\chi u)=[P,\chi]u.
\tag{F.10.4c.19.3}
$$

Its support is compact inside the Cauchy neighborhood. Retarded uniqueness gives $G_{\mathrm{ret}}F'=\chi u$ and advanced uniqueness gives $G_{\mathrm{adv}}F'=(\chi-1)u$, because these are respectively the solutions with vanishing past and future Cauchy data. Hence $EF'=u=EF$. Equivalently,
$F-F'=P(G_{\mathrm{ret}}F-\chi u)$,
with the expression in parentheses compactly supported in $O$; its tails vanish by the same retarded/advanced support identities. The on-shell map annihilates $P$ of a compact test, so $\kappa F=\kappa F'$. Every generator of $\mathfrak A(O)$ is therefore a generator from that Cauchy neighborhood. The reverse inclusion is isotony.

Finally apply (F.10.4c.16.4) to each of the two products in the commutator. Their ideal products agree by locality, giving (F.10.4c.19.2). The finite global cutoff and lattice dispersion retain their finite defects; the convergence and bound are on precisely the declared representation and state class. ∎

The represented time evolution is strongly continuous on each vector for bounded observables, by conjugation with the strongly continuous $U(t)$. Full real Weyl generators retain the norm-two separation and point-norm obstruction of Theorem F.0l. The finite corner maps, strong local-response limit and weakly closed net in (F.10.4c.19.1) give a topology-specific comparison record. They make no norm-inductive identification of the full Weyl algebra.

**Complete instruments and refinement responses.**

The common compared record uses the declared logical query labels and every quantum operation outcome, including failures. Each regulator also keeps its actual service timestamps, clock indices and resource inventory. Those deterministic regulator labels are compared to an ideal shadow carrying the same labels, or retained as auxiliary metadata; distinct deterministic timestamps are not assigned a vanishing total-variation distance. The clock-rounding estimates compare the quantum responses at the labeled queries. A contraction readout can be used either as a bounded expectation query or as a recorded operation. For the latter, define the finite success/failure isometry

$$
\mathcal V_{n,h}\xi
=K_n(h)\xi\otimes|0\rangle+
{(I-{K_n(h)}^*K_n(h))}^{1/2}\xi\otimes|1\rangle.
\tag{F.10.4c.20.1}
$$

Both records are preserved. Its ideal counterpart is $\mathcal V_h\psi=W(h)\psi\otimes|0\rangle$.

<a id="proposition-f104c20-complete-gaussian-instrument-responses"></a>**Proposition F.10.4c.20 (Complete Gaussian Instrument Responses).** For every finite adaptive protocol made of the declared source Weyl instruments, finite waits, vacuum preparation and bounded final effects, its full record distribution and final state converge to those of the corresponding ideal protocol. If the ideal input has $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\mathsf K)\le E$ and all ideal branch prefixes obey the finite bounds of Lemma F.10.4c.14, their trace-norm difference is at most $C(1+\sqrt E)2^{-n}$. The constant includes the number of retained operations and the indicated test/time budgets. Every cutoff-failure record is included in this bound. Two different regulators $n,k$ applied to the same declared protocol have response difference at most the sum of their respective bounds.

*Proof.* For $\psi$ already in $\operatorname{ran}Q_n$, the squared failure amplitude is exactly

$$
{\|{(I-K_n^*K_n)}^{1/2}I_n^*\psi\|}^2
={\|(I-Q_n)W(h_n^c)\psi\|}^2.
\tag{F.10.4c.20.2}
$$

For a general ideal input $\psi$, extend the finite isometry to $\mathcal H$ by adding a separate outside-code flag carrying $(I-Q_n)\psi$. Its success output is $Q_nW(h_n^c)Q_n\psi$. The success difference from $W(h)\psi$ is bounded by the right side $e_n(h,\psi)$ of (F.10.4c.16.1). By inserting $W(h)\psi$ and $W(h_n^c)\psi$, (F.10.4c.20.2) bounds the finite failure amplitude by the same $e_n$. The outside-code amplitude is at most $e_n$ as well. Their record sectors are orthogonal, so the extended Stinespring error is at most $\sqrt3e_n$.

Compose isometries and use the ideal-prefix/finite-suffix expansion of (F.10.4c.16.4). Isometries and channels contract the relevant norm; local errors are tested on ideal states, whose regularity is controlled by Lemma F.10.4c.14. Taking a partial trace converts a pure-vector error $\eta$ into trace-norm error at most $2\eta$. Mixtures are handled by purification or a spectral decomposition and Cauchy–Schwarz. The initial state channel (F.10.4c.16.5), after decoding, differs from $\rho$ in trace norm by at most $2\sqrt{\lambda_n}+\lambda_n$, where $\lambda_n=\operatorname{Tr}((I-Q_n)\rho)\le q_n^2E$: the first term is the elementary gentle projection bound, and the added vacuum has trace norm $\lambda_n$. This is also summable. Subsequent completely positive trace-preserving maps contract trace norm. Adaptation is implemented by record-controlled isometries; the finitely many ideal prefixes have their stated form budgets, and the same argument applies branchwise or to the coherent record register. Taking a final effect or reading all records cannot increase trace distance. Finally compare both regulators to the same ideal response and apply the triangle inequality. ∎

For clarity about the gentle projection step, purify $\rho$ to a unit vector $\Psi$ and put $\Psi_Q=(Q_n\otimes I)\Psi$. Then $\|\Psi-\Psi_Q\|=\sqrt{\lambda_n}$ and
${\||\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|-|\Psi_Q\rangle\langle\Psi_Q|\|}_1\le(\|\Psi\|+\|\Psi_Q\|)\|\Psi-\Psi_Q\|\le2\sqrt{\lambda_n}$.
Partial trace proves the quoted bound.

This is response refinement through one common ideal comparison, with explicit maps (F.10.4c.10.1)–(F.10.4c.10.2), source states (F.10.4c.16.5), source dynamics (F.10.4c.7.4) and complete instruments (F.10.4c.20.1). It does not require nested centered momentum cells or identify finite regulator algebras by a hidden isometric inductive system.

<a id="definition-f104c21-finite-gaussian-control-and-readout-record"></a>**Definition F.10.4c.21 (Finite Gaussian Control and Readout Record).**

The source-control model is a finite quantum register with calibrated finite Hermitian controls, a time standard and a retained classical measurement record. It uses the occupation encoding (F.10.4c.7.3), the same Hamiltonian (F.10.4c.7.4) and the same source matrices (F.10.4c.7.5), (F.10.4c.7.10) and (F.10.4c.20.1). Source responses are thereby attached to a specified finite carrier and finite interventions. Resource accounting in this section refers to control and readout costs; the field has no electromagnetic charge.

A finite executable protocol record contains:

1. $n,d$, the mass-computation record, the occupation encoding and vacuum label;
2. effectively supplied compact test functions or spatial Schwartz tests, their support/seminorm enclosures and target response tolerances;
3. the actual clock indices, matrices, ancillas, pulse or gate descriptions, and approximation enclosures;
4. the list of retained success/failure outcomes and the final effects;
5. the preparation, control, readout, sampling, memory and reset budgets below.

The all-test mathematical assertions in Definition F.10.4c.10 through Proposition F.10.4c.20 apply to arbitrary smooth tests. Algorithmic construction of a protocol requires the effective descriptions in item 2. A finite analytic constant exists for every admitted test; a numerical bound is computed when those input enclosures are supplied.

<a id="proposition-f104c22-positive-finite-hamiltonian-source-controls"></a>**Proposition F.10.4c.22 (Positive Finite-Hamiltonian Source Controls).** Every finite unitary or finite instrument used above has a unitary realization on finitely many source/ancilla qubits. It can be implemented in one declared service interval $\tau_n$ by the following calibrated finite control model. The code-space baseline is

$$
H_{0,n}=\nu_nI+H_n\otimes I_{\mathrm{anc}},\qquad \nu_n=4\pi/\tau_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.22.1}
$$

For the desired unitary $V$, let $R(t)=e^{-itH_{0,n}}$ and choose Hermitian $G$ with
$e^{-iG}={R(\tau_n)}^*V$ and $\|G\|\le2\pi$.
For $s(t)=3{(t/\tau_n)}^2-2{(t/\tau_n)}^3$ put

$$
C(t)=\dot s(t)R(t)G{R(t)}^*,\qquad 0\le t\le\tau_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.22.2}
$$

The physical propagator of $H_{0,n}+C(t)$ ends at $V$, and

$$
H_{0,n}+C(t)\ge\pi\tau_n^{-1}I,
\quad \sup_t\|C(t)\|\le3\pi/\tau_n,
\quad \int_0^{\tau_n}\|C(t)\|dt\le2\pi,
\quad \sup_t\|H_{0,n}+C(t)\|\le E_n^{\max}+7\pi/\tau_n.
\tag{F.10.4c.22.3}
$$

Free clock waits have propagator $e^{-ik\tau_nH_n}$ on the code because $e^{-ik\tau_n\nu_n}=1$; their Heisenberg action is exactly $U_n(k\tau_n)A{U_n(k\tau_n)}^*$. Every service interval and every free wait appears in the protocol clock record.

*Proof.* Finite-dimensional spectral calculus provides $G$. For effective implementation choose a branch cut off the finite spectrum of ${R(\tau_n)}^*V$, with angle in $(-2\pi,0)$, certified by a positive spectral gap. Such a cut exists; rational trial cuts and successively tighter spectral enclosures find one. The resulting logarithm has angles in an interval contained in $(-2\pi,2\pi)$ and is computable by continuous functional calculus on a neighborhood of the spectrum. The propagator is explicitly $R(t)e^{-is(t)G}$: differentiation gives the generator $H_{0,n}+C(t)$ and the endpoint is $R(\tau_n)e^{-iG}=V$. Since $0\le\dot s\le3/(2\tau_n)$, all bounds in (F.10.4c.22.3) follow from $\|G\|\le2\pi$, $H_n\ge0$, and $\int\dot s=1$. ∎

For a contraction $A$ the explicit Halmos dilation is

$$
\mathcal U(A)=
\begin{pmatrix}
A&{(I-AA^*)}^{1/2}\\
{(I-A^*A)}^{1/2}&-A^*
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{F.10.4c.22.4}
$$

It is unitary: the diagonal blocks of $\mathcal U(A){\mathcal U(A)}^*$ are identities and the off-diagonal blocks vanish by

$$
A{(I-A^*A)}^{1/2}={(I-AA^*)}^{1/2}A.
$$

The latter identity first holds for polynomials by $A{(A^*A)}^r={(AA^*)}^rA$ and then for the square root by uniform polynomial approximation on $[0,1]$. Input ancilla $|0\rangle$ gives (F.10.4c.20.1). This also realizes a transfer contraction $e^{-sH_n}$ without interpreting it as autonomous unitary time evolution.

For a word of $k$ contractions, use a fresh flag ancilla for each factor. The all-zero block of the product dilation is exactly the product of contractions. A controlled version plus one interferometer qubit measures its real or imaginary expectation. No postselection is used: the bounded interferometric outcome is averaged over every trial. If a protocol instead requests the state conditioned on successful Euclidean transfer, its success probability is at least $e^{-2sE_n^{\max}}$ and its repetition and normalization error must be included explicitly. The present response grammar uses the unconditioned measurement or the complete instrument.

The external controller owns the control work and the clock/ancilla/readout services. Since $C(0)=C(\tau_n)=0$, the net work on the closed finite register during one service pulse equals its endpoint change in $\langle H_{0,n}\rangle$; its absolute value is at most $E_n^{\max}$, with the same bound for the padded zero-energy extension and degenerate ancillas. This endpoint work, the integrated control norm in (F.10.4c.22.3), the clock service and any ancilla reset are distinct resource entries. The finite matrix-history functional in (F.10.4c.8.4) is evaluated by such contractions. For a field factor use
$\beta_{n,h}=\max\{1,2\sqrt{R_n+1}\|h\|\}$ and dilate $\phi_n(h)/\beta_{n,h}$, which is a contraction by the number bound. The product normalization $B_{n,w}=\prod_j\beta_{n,h_j}$ is restored in the reported raw moment and in its statistical error. This factor is never omitted from the cost of estimating high moments.

**The resource and error record.**

At regulator $n$, a $k$-query protocol needs $q_n^{\mathrm{code}}=\lceil\log_2D_n\rceil$ source qubits, at most $k$ flag ancillas and one interferometer qubit, plus any explicitly supplied preparation/work ancillas. A direct dense pulse on the combined carrier has at most the square of that carrier dimension in real control coefficients. It occupies one service interval $\tau_n$ per requested unitary; free encoded field waits occupy their actual $|k|\tau_n$ intervals. Negative logical waits and controlled waits use the declared pulse implementation, with their baseline phase compensated by (F.10.4c.22.2). Lattice spatial labels are encoded field coordinates. The source control layout and service overhead have their own recorded coordinates and times; they are not identified with a microscopic geometric light cone.

A digital alternative decomposes the finite dilations into two-level unitaries, then into one-qubit gates and CNOTs. QR elimination uses at most $D'(D'-1)/2$ two-level elimination factors and $D'$ diagonal phase factors for a $D'$-dimensional unitary. The finite gate construction of Barenco et al. gives a finite elementary circuit for each such factor on the padded qubit space. Fix a finite inverse-closed universal alphabet for $SU(2)$ and use the Solovay–Kitaev algorithm to approximate the determinant-one parts of those elementary rotations. Scalar phases, including relative phases on controlled arms, are retained separately and implemented by the calibrated dense-pulse phase control (F.10.4c.22.2). Record the actual compiled gate count $G_{n,w}$ and target gate accuracy; circuit existence and finite cost follow from these constructions. No efficiency or polynomial-in-volume cost is asserted. The dense-pulse realization already supplies an explicit finite alternative when an elementary gate decomposition is not retained.

Put $\eta_n=2^{-n}$. For a bounded query set $B_{n,w}=1$; for a raw field moment retain its normalization product above. Allocate the normalized tolerance $\widehat\eta_{n,w}=\eta_n/B_{n,w}$. Let the unitary implementation error for each service operation be at most $\widehat\eta_{n,w}/(8k)$ in operator norm, the input preparation trace error at most $\widehat\eta_{n,w}/4$, and the total readout-channel error at most $\widehat\eta_{n,w}/4$. For a digital circuit it suffices to enclose each primitive gate error by $\widehat\eta_{n,w}/(8kG_{n,w})$. For the pulse model it suffices to certify

$$
\int_0^{\tau_n}\|H_{\mathrm{actual}}(t)-H_{0,n}-C(t)\|dt
\le\widehat\eta_{n,w}/(8k).
\tag{F.10.4c.22.5}
$$

Duhamel's identity bounds the corresponding propagator norm error by that integral. Clock error is included: replacing a free wait $t$ by $t+\Delta t$ has operator error at most $|\Delta t|E_n^{\max}$, and an implemented service waveform uses its full Hamiltonian norm bound in (F.10.4c.22.3). These are finite source-control tolerances; the separate continuum clock error has already been paid in Lemma F.10.4c.15. Unitary errors bound channel trace errors by twice their operator error, so telescoping gives a total normalized implementation trace error at most $\widehat\eta_{n,w}$, hence raw-response bias at most $\eta_n$, with room in the allocation for padding and phase controls.

For a bounded real response in $[-1,1]$, $N_{n,w}$ independent trials give additive sampling error at most $\eta_n$ with failure probability at most $\zeta_n$ when

$$
N_{n,w}\ge2\eta_n^{-2}\log(2/\zeta_n).
\tag{F.10.4c.22.6}
$$

For both real and imaginary parts, use $\log(4/\zeta_n)$ and two batches. For a raw field moment multiply the sample requirement by $B_{n,w}^2$ and apply the bound to the normalized response. Set $\zeta_n=\zeta2^{-n}$, so $\sum_{n\ge1}\zeta_n=\zeta$. With probability at least $1-\zeta$, every retained stage satisfies its sampling bound. The source record includes all trial outcomes; $N_{n,w}$ trials of $k$ two-outcome flags and one readout require at most $N_{n,w}(k+1)$ raw classical bits per real batch. A requested irreversible reset of those bits has its supplied reservoir and work/heat budget; at temperature $T_b$ the ordinary entropy-erasure floor is $k_BT_b$ times their erased Shannon entropy. The response proof requires no reset and may retain the record instead. Additional state preparation cost is an explicit $C_{\mathrm{prep},n}$ input; vacuum preparation is the designated zero-occupation codeword.

For a fixed complete instrument protocol, its trace error is the analytic bound in Proposition F.10.4c.20 plus its implementation error. For an expectation estimator, the continuum bias is the applicable analytic response bound (or the fixed-degree moment bound (F.10.4c.17.7)), plus raw implementation bias at most $\eta_n$ and raw sampling error at most $\eta_n$. These sums are summable on (F.10.4c.7.1). The $n$-dependent archive of $N_{n,w}$ independent trials is a growing protocol: (F.10.4c.22.6) certifies its estimator around the implemented expectation, after which the continuum bias is added. Proposition F.10.4c.20's fixed-length complete-record trace bound is not assigned unchanged to that entire growing archive; a full-archive comparison would pay its actual repetition factor. Register, ancilla, pulse strength, pulse integral, source energy, service time, coefficient precision, gate count if used, sample count, record storage and any reset are all separate entries. The formal finite source realization is supplied by (F.10.4c.7.3)–(F.10.4c.8.4) and (F.10.4c.20.1)–(F.10.4c.22.6). Each finite run retains those instantiated control and resource entries.

<a id="remark-f104c24-reconstruction-and-control-sources"></a>**Remark F.10.4c.24 (Reconstruction and Control Sources).**

The Gaussian reconstruction and finite-source estimates above use the following reconstruction background and finite-control results.

- Osterwalder and Schrader (1973, 1975). The corrected reconstruction treatment of the 1975 paper is the relevant general background. Theorem F.10.4c.18 separately proves field domains and temperedness, so reflection positivity is not used as a substitute for those hypotheses.
- Jaffe (2015, Section II). It exhibits the Gaussian covariance and full reflection-quotient framework. Theorems F.10.4c.17–F.10.4c.18 provide the explicit maps for the source selected here.
- Arici et al. (2018). Its rational-covariance reflection classification is already the comparison source of Theorem F.10.4c.6.
- Barenco et al. (1995). The imported statement is finite universality of one-qubit gates and CNOT, including multi-controlled gate constructions.
- Dawson and Nielsen (2006). The imported statement is finite fixed-alphabet approximation of one-qubit rotations with a certified accuracy; the actual compiled count is retained in the optional digital record.
- Jordan et al. (2014). It provides relevant finite-register lattice-field context; none of its scattering or efficiency claims are used as premises of this construction.

### F.10.4d Minimal Gauge Split-Factorization

<a id="definition-f104d1-finite-gauge-split-datum"></a>**Definition F.10.4d.1 (Finite Gauge-Split Datum).** A finite gauge-split datum for a region $R$ is a quadruple
$$
(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}},\mathfrak A_R,\mathfrak A_{\bar R},Z_{\partial R})
$$
where $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}$ is a finite-dimensional physical Hilbert space after imposing gauge constraints, $\mathfrak A_R$ and $\mathfrak A_{\bar R}$ are commuting finite-dimensional von Neumann algebras of gauge-invariant observables, and
$$
Z_{\partial R}
=
\mathfrak A_R\cap\mathfrak A_{\bar R}
$$
is their common finite-dimensional center. The datum is locally complete when, on each minimal central block, $\mathfrak A_R$ and $\mathfrak A_{\bar R}$ are mutual commutants and generate the full matrix algebra of that block.

<a id="theorem-f104d2-minimal-gauge-split-factorization"></a>**Theorem F.10.4d.2 (Minimal Gauge Split-Factorization).** Let $(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}},\mathfrak A_R,\mathfrak A_{\bar R},Z_{\partial R})$ be a locally complete finite gauge-split datum. Let
$$
1=\sum_{\alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}Z_{\partial R}}p_\alpha
$$
be the decomposition into minimal central projections. Then there are finite Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_R^\alpha$ and $\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha$ such that
$$
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}
\cong
\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}Z_{\partial R}}
\mathcal H_R^\alpha\otimes\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha,
\tag{F.10.4d.1}
$$
and, under this isomorphism,
$$
\mathfrak A_R
\cong
\bigoplus_\alpha
B(\mathcal H_R^\alpha)\otimes I_{\bar R}^\alpha,
\qquad
\mathfrak A_{\bar R}
\cong
\bigoplus_\alpha
I_R^\alpha\otimes B(\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha).
\tag{F.10.4d.2}
$$
The central syndrome labels $\alpha\in\operatorname{Spec}Z_{\partial R}$ index the common blocks needed to assemble the two local observable algebras. They do not determine a joint state from its two local marginals; joint correlations within each tensor-product block remain additional state data.

*Proof.* Since $Z_{\partial R}$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $C^*$-algebra, it has a unique decomposition into minimal central projections:
$$
Z_{\partial R}\cong\bigoplus_\alpha \mathbb C p_\alpha,
\qquad
1=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha.
$$
Thus
$$
\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}
=
\bigoplus_\alpha p_\alpha\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}.
$$
Fix one block $\mathcal H_\alpha=p_\alpha\mathcal H_{\mathrm{phys}}$. The compressed algebras
$$
\mathfrak A_R^\alpha=p_\alpha\mathfrak A_Rp_\alpha,
\qquad
\mathfrak A_{\bar R}^\alpha=p_\alpha\mathfrak A_{\bar R}p_\alpha
$$
are finite factors by minimality of $p_\alpha$ in the common center. Local completeness says
$$
(\mathfrak A_R^\alpha)'=\mathfrak A_{\bar R}^\alpha,
\qquad
(\mathfrak A_{\bar R}^\alpha)'=\mathfrak A_R^\alpha,
\qquad
\mathfrak A_R^\alpha\vee\mathfrak A_{\bar R}^\alpha=B(\mathcal H_\alpha).
$$
The finite-dimensional bicommutant structure theorem for mutual factor commutants then gives Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_R^\alpha$ and $\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha$ with
$$
\mathcal H_\alpha\cong\mathcal H_R^\alpha\otimes\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha,
$$
$$
\mathfrak A_R^\alpha\cong B(\mathcal H_R^\alpha)\otimes I_{\bar R}^\alpha,
\qquad
\mathfrak A_{\bar R}^\alpha\cong I_R^\alpha\otimes B(\mathcal H_{\bar R}^\alpha).
$$
Taking the direct sum over $\alpha$ proves (F.10.4d.1) and (F.10.4d.2). ∎

<a id="corollary-f104d3-pce-minimal-edge-data-in-gauge-theory"></a>**Corollary F.10.4d.3 (PCE-Minimal Edge Data in Gauge Theory).** In a locally complete finite gauge-split datum, compare the center $Z_{\partial R}$ only with its proper refinements that leave every retained prediction unchanged. Assume the complete PCE potential strictly increases under each such refinement. One sufficient certificate is a strictly positive coefficient multiplying the increased description cost, with every other contribution to that potential unchanged. Then no proper refinement in this comparison class minimizes the potential; the center is its unique minimizing response representative. This claim does not exclude a sufficient coarsening for a particular state and protocol class.

*Proof.* Theorem F.10.4d.2 supplies the common-block decomposition of the observable algebras. For every proper refinement in the stated comparison class, the complete potential is strictly larger than at $Z_{\partial R}$ by hypothesis. Hence the center has lower potential than every other member of that class. In the sufficient additive certificate, the positive cost increment times its positive coefficient is exactly the potential difference because all other terms cancel. No comparison with coarsenings or with state correlations is implied. ∎

### F.10.4e De Finetti Field Emergence

<a id="definition-f104e1-exchangeable-mpu-ensemble"></a>**Definition F.10.4e.1 (Exchangeable MPU Ensemble).** Let $\mathcal K$ be the finite single-carrier Hilbert space of an MPU-local retained sector. A consistent exchangeable MPU ensemble is a family of states
$$
\rho_N\in B(\mathcal K^{\otimes N})_*,
\qquad N=1,2,\dots,
$$
such that:

1. $\rho_N$ is invariant under every permutation of the $N$ tensor factors;
2. tracing out the last $N-k$ factors of $\rho_N$ gives $\rho_k$ for every $k<N$.

<a id="theorem-f104e2-fields-as-extremal-exchangeable-predictive-components"></a>**Theorem F.10.4e.2 (Fields as Extremal Exchangeable Predictive Components).** For every consistent exchangeable MPU ensemble there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the compact state space $\mathcal S(\mathcal K)$ such that for every fixed $k$,
$$
\rho_k
=
\int_{\mathcal S(\mathcal K)}
\sigma^{\otimes k}\,d\mu(\sigma).
\tag{F.10.4e.1}
$$
The extremal exchangeable components are exactly the product families $\sigma^{\otimes k}$, and the measure $\mu$ is the branch-level field-mixture measure.

*Proof.* The carrier algebra is the finite-dimensional complex matrix algebra $B(\mathcal K)$. Consistency under partial trace defines a state on its countable tensor-product algebra, and finite-permutation invariance makes that state symmetric. Theorem 7 of Ligthart, Gachechiladze, and Gross (2023) gives a unique probability measure on the single-site state space and its product-state representation; for a matrix algebra the minimal and maximal finite tensor-product norms coincide. Consequently there is a unique Borel probability measure $\mu$ on the compact state space $\mathcal S(\mathcal K)$, and
$$
\rho_k=\int_{\mathcal S(\mathcal K)}\sigma^{\otimes k}\,d\mu(\sigma)
$$
for every $k$.

Suppose first that $\mu$ is not a point mass. Because $\mathcal S(\mathcal K)$ is a compact metric space, there is a Borel set $A$ with $0<\mu(A)<1$. Put $\lambda=\mu(A)$ and define
$$
\mu_1(B)=\frac{\mu(B\cap A)}{\lambda},
\qquad
\mu_2(B)=\frac{\mu(B\cap A^c)}{1-\lambda}.
$$
Then $\mu=\lambda\mu_1+(1-\lambda)\mu_2$. Integrating $\sigma^{\otimes k}$ gives two consistent exchangeable families $\rho^{(1)}$ and $\rho^{(2)}$ with
$$
\rho=\lambda\rho^{(1)}+(1-\lambda)\rho^{(2)}.
$$
The representing measures $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are distinct, so uniqueness of the de Finetti measure makes the two families distinct. Thus $\rho$ is not extremal.

Conversely, let $\mu=\delta_\sigma$ and suppose
$$
\rho=\lambda\tau+(1-\lambda)\omega,
\qquad 0<\lambda<1,
$$
for exchangeable families $\tau$ and $\omega$ with representing measures $\nu_\tau$ and $\nu_\omega$. Uniqueness gives
$$
\delta_\sigma=\lambda\nu_\tau+(1-\lambda)\nu_\omega.
$$
For the complement of $\{\sigma\}$, both nonnegative terms have sum zero, so both measures are supported at $\sigma$ and hence equal $\delta_\sigma$. Uniqueness again gives $\tau=\omega=\rho$. Therefore the product family $\sigma^{\otimes k}$ is extremal, and the extremal families are exactly the product families. ∎

<a id="corollary-f104e3-finite-approximation-bound"></a>**Corollary F.10.4e.3 (Finite Approximation Bound).** If only an $N$-carrier symmetric state is available, then for every $k<N$ there exists a probability measure $\mu_{N,k}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathcal K)$ such that
$$
\left\|
\rho_{N,k}
-
\int\sigma^{\otimes k}\,d\mu_{N,k}(\sigma)
\right\|_1
\le
\frac{4(\dim\mathcal K)^2k}{N},
\tag{F.10.4e.2}
$$
where $\rho_{N,k}$ is the $k$-carrier marginal.

*Proof.* Apply Christandl et al. (2007, Theorem II.7) to the permutation-invariant state $\rho_N$ on $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes N}$, where $d=\dim\mathcal K$. The source uses the trace distance $D(\rho,\sigma)=\tfrac12\|\rho-\sigma\|_1$ and bounds the $k$-body distance to a convex mixture of product states by $2d^2k/N$. Multiplying by $2$ gives the displayed ordinary trace-norm bound
$$
\frac{4d^2k}{N}.
$$
If this bound exceeds the maximal ordinary trace-norm distance $2$ between states, the assertion is automatic. ∎

<a id="corollary-f104e4-regular-field-branch"></a>**Corollary F.10.4e.4 (Regular Field Branch).** Let the de Finetti measure $\mu$ be supported on the image of a Borel parametrization $\phi\mapsto\sigma_\phi$ of a regular finite-dimensional family. Assume a Borel probability measure $\nu$ on $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has been supplied with pushforward $\sigma_*\nu=\mu$. For bounded one-site observables,
$$
